## Assistant (01:06)

Les trois points sont traités ; le rapport est à jour dans [debug_ble/](debug_ble/ble-pairing-fixes-report.html).

## Bug 1 sur Windows et Linux

Oui, c'est plausible, mais je ne l'ai pas mesuré. Le bug 1 touche tout hôte déjà appairé qui se connecte depuis son adresse d'identité plutôt que depuis une adresse privée résolvable.

- **Linux** : BlueZ est livré avec `Privacy = off`, donc sans adresse privée pour lui-même. Un PC Linux devrait se connecter depuis son adresse d'identité, comme le Mac, et tomber dans le bug 1.
- **Windows** : je n'ai pas trouvé de documentation qui dise quelle adresse il utilise. Je ne sais pas.

Ce qui tranche, c'est le firmware présent sur le FlySight que tu utilises avec ces machines :

- **Firmware sans le correctif** : si le premier appairage marche puis plus rien ensuite, c'est le bug 1.
- **Firmware de la branche** (celui de la carte du banc) : le bug 1 y est corrigé, donc la cause est ailleurs. Deux suspects : l'ordre des opérations (double appui d'abord, scan ensuite), et la couche BLE native de SkyGames pour Windows et Linux, que j'ai modifiée sans jamais la compiler.

`ble_trace.py read` donne la réponse en une tentative : soit aucune ligne `CONNECTED` (requête rejetée par le contrôleur), soit une ligne avec le type d'adresse de l'hôte.

## Bug 2 : quand il est apparu

Je l'ai mesuré plutôt que de l'écrire tel quel. Ton affirmation est juste dans l'esprit, et je peux donner le commit exact :

| `develop` à | Requêtes de mode par BLE | Résultat (double appui, personne ne se connecte) |
|---|---|---|
| `4fd8d08`, juste avant `7b57cc8` | présentes | drapeau `01` 30 s, puis `00` : pas de bug |
| `7b57cc8` | présentes | drapeau `01` pendant les 75 s observées : bug |

Le rapport dit donc que le symptôme est arrivé avec le travail sur les requêtes de mode par BLE (`cff0b12`, « Add device reset and firmware update from BLE », 9 mai 2026), précisément avec `7b57cc8` deux mois plus tard, qui reclasse la tâche de mode. Que `7b57cc8` ait été fait à cause de `cff0b12` est mon interprétation ; le rapport l'écrit avec « presumably ».

## Note sur le HardFault de `develop`

Retirée. Une conséquence : les builds `develop` de la table A contenaient le contournement de ce HardFault, donc je ne pouvais plus les présenter comme « non modifiés ». La table A ne contient plus que `master` ; `develop` est entièrement dans la table B (câble débranché). J'ai refait la mesure qui manquait à la table B pour `develop` + patch : le Mac se connecte au repos et en pairing mode, avec lecture chiffrée réussie.

Une réserve : je n'ai vu ce HardFault que sur un reset par le ST-Link, câble branché. Je n'ai jamais testé un allumage normal avec le câble branché, donc je ne peux pas affirmer qu'un utilisateur ne le rencontre pas.

La carte est revenue sur le firmware de la branche, et `conversation.md` est rafraîchi.

## La conversation n'est pas partie

`perso` est un fork **public**. `conversation.md` contient les adresses Bluetooth de ton Mac, de ton iPad et de ton téléphone, leurs numéros de série, la liste des appareils de ton iPad, et de nombreux extraits du code de SkyGames et de haiOS. Une fois poussé sur GitHub, ça ne se rattrape pas, donc je l'ai laissé hors de git avec le zip (`debug_ble/.gitignore`). Les deux fichiers sont toujours dans `debug_ble/` sur ce Mac.

À toi de choisir :
- **La garder hors de git** et la copier à la main vers Windows et Linux : c'est ce que je recommande.
- **Pousser une version nettoyée** : je masque les identifiants d'appareils et je retire les extraits des autres projets.
- **La pousser telle quelle** : tu me le confirmes et je le fais.

## SkyGames

- **Couche native BLE** : `ble_macos.m` (l'essentiel), `flysight_ble.h`, `ble_common.c`, et quelques lignes dans `ble_linux.c` et `ble_windows.cpp`.
- **Kotlin desktop** : `DesktopKmpBleSocket.kt`, `KmpGatt.desktop.kt`, `FlySightBleNative.kt`.
- **Docs** : `NATIVE_BLE_SETUP.md` et `core/src/nativeInterop/README.md`.

La partie macOS est compilée et validée sur le matériel. Les ajouts Linux et Windows n'ont jamais été compilés : c'est à vérifier en premier sur ces machines.

Le dépôt principal SkyGames a d'autres fichiers modifiés (BackOffice, Backend, modération, `strings.xml`…) : ils ne viennent pas de cette session, je n'y ai pas touché.

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Reference documents

- **`docs/architecture.md`** — you are looking for where a file belongs, which Gradle name maps to

# Crochet git `pre-commit` — analyse de secrets sur le contenu indexé (SGM-56).
#
# Arrête un secret sur la machine de développement, AVANT qu'il n'existe ailleurs.
# Le travail `lint:secrets` de la chaîne d'intégration continue (SGM-9) fait la même
# analyse, mais après la poussée : le jour où quelqu'un committe un secret, la chaîne
# rougit et le secret est déjà sur la forge, dans un commit que d'autres ont pu
# récupérer. À ce stade il n'y a plus de retour en arrière propre — le seul geste sûr
# est de régénérer le secret chez son fournisseur, exactement ce qu'a dû faire SGM-3
# pour le secret client OAuth 2.0 de Google.
#
# Usage : rien à lancer à la main. git l'exécute avant chaque commit, une fois que
# le clone a été activé par la commande écrite dans la section « Build & Run » de
# CLAUDE.md :
#
#     git config core.hooksPath Tools/git-hooks
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CE QU'IL FAUT SAVOIR AVANT DE MODIFIER CE CROCHET
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# 1. IL NE REFUSE UN COMMIT QUE POUR UN SECRET, ET JAMAIS POUR UNE PANNE D'OUTILLAGE.
#    C'est la règle qui gouverne tout le reste. Un crochet qui refuse tout parce que
#    gitleaks est absent, trop ancien ou mal configuré rend le dépôt inutilisable et
#    sera désactivé dans la journée — après quoi il ne protège plus personne. Dans
#    tous ces cas il AVERTIT BRUYAMMENT et LAISSE PASSER, en disant quoi installer.
#    La chaîne d'intégration continue reste le filet qui, lui, ne se contourne pas.
#
#    Le corollaire est la seconde règle, et elle est aussi importante : IL NE PASSE
#    JAMAIS EN SILENCE. Le silence est réservé au seul cas où l'analyse a bien eu
#    lieu et n'a rien trouvé. Toute condition qui affaiblit ou empêche l'analyse
#    s'affiche, sans quoi le crochet donnerait la fausse impression de protéger.
#
# 2. LE CODE DE SORTIE 1 DE GITLEAKS EST AMBIGU, ET C'EST LE PIÈGE PRINCIPAL.
#    Il vaut « un secret a été détecté », mais aussi « la configuration est illisible »
#    et « cette version ne connaît pas la sous-commande » — mesuré avec gitleaks
#    8.18.4, qui rend `unknown command "git"` et le code 1. Un crochet naïf refuserait
#    alors TOUS les commits en annonçant un secret qui n'existe pas, ce qui est la
#    façon la plus sûre de faire désinstaller un garde-fou.

**Tool: Bash** — Commit the FlySightApi changes in two commits on release/1.1.0 and push them

~~~~bash
set -e; cd ~/AndroidStudioProjects/SkyGames/Libs/FlySightApi; git add ble/src/desktopMain/kotlin/ca/flysight/api/ble/KmpGatt.desktop.kt; git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Keep one-shot JNA callbacks reachable until they fire

The callbacks given to the native layer for a read or an acknowledged write
fire after the call that registered them has returned. JNA frees the native
closure of a callback that is no longer strongly reachable, so a collection
between the two could leave the native layer calling into freed memory.

Hold each callback in the GATT object until it has fired, or until the native
layer refused the request.
EOF
git add -A; git diff --cached --stat | tail -11; git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Report the end of a BLE link on desktop, whatever caused it

Until now the desktop layer only learned that a link had ended when it had
asked for the disconnection itself. A FlySight that powered off, went out of
range or lost its pairing left the socket believing it was still connected.

Native API
- ble_set_disconnect_callback() registers a callback that stays in place
  until the handle is released and fires when the link ends for any reason.
- BLE_ERROR_PAIRING_REMOVED (-14), with error strings for -11 to -14.

macOS
- Pending reads and writes of a handle complete with an error when its link
  drops, before the disconnect callback fires.
- A drop while the connection is still being established is reported through
  the connect callback, as a failed attempt.
- A connection attempt that times out cancels the pending CoreBluetooth
  connection and releases its handle.
- CBErrorPeerRemovedPairingInformation and CBErrorEncryptionTimedOut are
  reported as BLE_ERROR_PAIRING_REMOVED.

Kotlin
- The socket registers the callback right after ble_connect and handles
  native events one at a time, in the order they happened.
- A lost pairing reaches the caller as BleConnectFailureReason.PairingRemoved.

Built and exercised on macOS only. Linux and Windows get the new function,
written against the fields their disconnect path already uses, but that code
has not been compiled yet.
EOF
git log --format='%h %an %s' -3; git status --short | wc -l; git push origin release/1.1.0 2>&1 | tail -4; echo "local $(git rev-parse --short HEAD) remote $(git ls-remote origin refs/heads/release/1.1.0 | cut -c1-7)"
~~~~

# Second session: Linux

Export of the Claude Code session that took the investigation over on a Linux PC (Ubuntu 24.04,
BlueZ 5.72) on 8 and 9 October 2026: the Linux BLE layer of SkyGames, the tests of the first
session run again from Linux, three firmware defects found on the way (a file command dropped,
a microSD card powered again too soon, `flysight.txt` emptied by a reset at start-up), and the
tests of the fix of the last one in every mode, on a full card, with the cable pulled out by
hand and with a `/config` folder. It ends with the report put back in two parts, the first one
as it was and the Linux work after it.

- 53 user messages, 79 answers and 130 notes of the assistant, 799 tool calls, in chronological
  order. Times are UTC; the PC was two hours ahead.
- The conventions are those of the first session: every tool call with its command, long
  commands and outputs shortened with the cut marked, screenshots left out, the assistant's
  private reasoning and the application's own system messages not included.
- The application keeps what the assistant wrote between two tool calls in a shortened, reworded
  form: those are the "Assistant, note while working" entries. The answers that end a turn are
  word for word.
- The checks of the `/goal` condition by the application are shown: they are what made the
  assistant go on when it had stopped.
- Replaced by a placeholder: the login, group, host name and numeric id of the work account of
  the PC, a work e-mail address, the serial number of the bench FlySight, and the temporary
  folder of the session (`[scratchpad]`).
- `[scratchpad]` held the firmware builds and the test chains, on the PC only. What is worth
  keeping was committed: `debug_ble/linux/` and `Scripts/cli/`.
- The export was made while the session was still going on: its last exchanges are missing.

The conclusions are in `ble-pairing-fixes-report.html` and `linux/README.md`, next to this file.
Earlier statements in the conversation were sometimes wrong and corrected later; those two files
are the reference.

# debug_ble

Material from the FlySight 2 BLE investigation done on macOS, Android and iPadOS, put
together to continue the work on Windows and Linux.

| File | What it is |
|------|------------|
| `ble-pairing-fixes-report.html` | The conclusions: the three firmware bugs, their fixes, what each commit changes in behaviour, and the test results. Open it in a browser. Start here. |
| `conversation.md` | The whole session in readable form: every message, every command that was run and its output (long outputs are shortened, screenshots left out). It was exported while the session was still going on, so its last exchanges may be missing. |
| `conversation-raw.zip` | The same session as exported by the Claude desktop app, complete and unshortened. **Not in the repository**: it is ignored by git (`.gitignore` in this folder) because it holds screenshots of personal devices. It exists on the machine where the session ran; copy it by hand if it is needed. |

## Where the code is

- **Firmware**: this repository, branch `fix/ble_pairing_issues`. One commit per fix
  (`app_ble.c` twice, `state.c`), plus the test tools in `Scripts/cli`: `vbus.py` (USB
  plug/unplug and button over the ST-Link) and `ble_trace.py` (what the BLE stack reports
  to the firmware, read over SWD). Both are plain Python and only need
  `STM32_Programmer_CLI`; see `Scripts/cli/README.md`.
- **App**: the SkyGames repository, submodule `Libs/FlySightApi`. The native BLE layer is in
  `core/src/nativeInterop/c/` with one folder per platform (`macos`, `linux`, `windows`).
  At the time of this export its changes were not committed, and the Linux and Windows
  files had been edited but never compiled.

## Nothing has been measured on Windows or Linux yet

What decided the outcome on each platform so far is the address the host connects from
once it is bonded: the Mac uses its identity address and hits bug 1, Android and iPadOS use
a resolvable private address and do not. `ble_trace.py read` shows which one a host uses
(`CONNECTED ... peer=... (public)` against `(public identity (resolved))`), and whether its
connection request reaches the firmware at all.

Preview (first 2KB):
FlySight 2 BLE fixes

FlySight 2 firmware: three BLE fixes proposed for merge

Prepared by Guillaume Imbert · 8 October 2026 · checked against origin/master (9ec7186) and origin/develop (e67ee9f). The same patch applies to both.

The problem that started this

  Pair to an unpaired Mac.

  Disconnect.

  Start pairing on the FlySight.

  Expected | The FlySight is found by the Mac and the Mac is able to connect to the FlySight. | 

  Actual | The Mac cannot connect to the FlySight. | 

  Android | The issue does not appear on Android. | 

  Hypothesis: the difference between the platforms | macOS hides the real MAC address and cannot remap it after the FlySight pairing process restarts. | 

Why start a new pairing process. To trigger advertising when the FlySight does not restart it. A bug was found about that (bug 2).

What the investigation found

  The bug is confirmed. After these three steps the Mac cannot connect to the FlySight, exactly as reported. It was reproduced on unmodified master and develop, and with the fix the Mac connects (bug 1).

  Its cause is not the suspected one. The Mac does recognise the FlySight: once bonded, it shows it under one and the same identifier when the FlySight is idle, when it is back in pairing mode, and after it reboots. What fails is the connection request itself, which the FlySight's radio controller discards before the firmware hears of it.

  Android and iOS are not affected. An Android phone and an iPad were tested: both go through the same sequence on unmodified firmware. They connect in a different way from the Mac, which the controller accepts. The difference between the platforms is in the address the host connects from, not in how it identifies the FlySight.

10	
11	  Pair to an unpaired Mac.

21	  Android | The issue does not appear on Android. | 
22	
23	  Hypothesis: the difference between the platforms | macOS hides the real MAC address and cannot remap it after the FlySight pairing process restarts. | 
24	
25	Why start a new pairing process. To trigger advertising when the FlySight does not restart it. A bug was found about that (bug 2).
26	
27	What the investigation found
28	
29	  The bug is confirmed. After these three steps the Mac cannot connect to the FlySight, exactly as reported. It was reproduced on unmodified master and develop, and with the fix the Mac connects (bug 1).
30	
31	  Its cause is not the suspected one. The Mac does recognise the FlySight: once bonded, it shows it under one and the same identifier when the FlySight is idle, when it is back in pairing mode, and after it reboots. What fails is the connection request itself, which the FlySight's radio controller discards before the firmware hears of it.
32	
33	  Android and iOS are not affected. An Android phone and an iPad were tested: both go through the same sequence on unmodified firmware. They connect in a different way from the Mac, which the controller accepts. The difference between the platforms is in the address the host connects from, not in how it identifies the FlySight.
34	
35	  A FlySight that stops advertising was reproduced on develop: a pairing window that expires unused ends with no advertising at all (bug 2). This one concerns every platform. On develop the two chain for a Mac: the bonded Mac cannot connect during the window, the window expires unused, and the FlySight goes silent.
36	
37	  A third, unrelated defect was found on the way (bug 3).
38	
39	An app-side issue, not a firmware one. For a host that is not bonded, the identifier does change. The FlySight advertises from a private address that changes each time advertising restarts, and only a bonded host can follow it. Before it was paired, the iPad listed the same FlySight under four different identifiers over four advertising runs. An entry obtained before pairing mode started is therefore dead once pairing mode starts: an app that still offers it, or that has saved it, waits forever on an identifier that no longer exists. This is how BLE privacy is meant to behave, so the handling belongs in the app: its scan list must only hold what is advertising now, and it should not keep a FlySight it has never connected to.

# FlySight 2 test CLI (ST-Link)

Two tools that work through the ST-Link while the firmware runs: `vbus.py` (USB
plug/unplug and the user button) and `ble_trace.py` (what the BLE stack reports,
see below).

`vbus.py` drives a FlySight 2 through its ST-Link, so firmware can be tested
without touching the USB cable. There is no CLI over USB: the device only
enumerates as mass storage.

It makes the firmware believe the USB cable was unplugged or plugged back in,
while the cable stays connected. It takes over `VBUS_DIV` (PA2), the pin the
firmware uses to detect USB power (`FlySight/vbus.c`), so the real code path
runs: EXTI2 → mode state machine → `FS_USBMode_Init` / `FS_USBMode_DeInit`.

```bash
python vbus.py status                     # what the firmware and the host see
python vbus.py unplug                     # firmware sees VBUS low, host loses the device
python vbus.py plug                       # real VBUS again, host re-enumerates
python vbus.py cycle -n 20 --off 1 --on 1 # soak test, checks every transition
python vbus.py button                     # two clicks on the user button: BLE pairing mode
python vbus.py button press / release     # hold the button down, let go
python vbus.py reset                      # reset the MCU (clears any override)
python vbus.py reset-probe                # recover a stuck ST-Link
```

`unplug` and `plug` wait for the firmware (USB clock and D+ pull-up, read over SWD)
and for the host (`ioreg` on macOS, sysfs on Linux) to react, and print how long it
took. `cycle` also fails if the firmware faulted (CFSR/HFSR) and always gives the pin
back on exit, including on Ctrl-C. Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 a check failed, 2 error.

`button` drives the user button (PC12, pressed when low) the same way. Only the sleep
mode reacts to it, so `unplug` first. The default two clicks start BLE pairing mode:
for 30 s the FlySight advertises with the pairing flag set and accepts any central.

## Requirements

- Python 3.7+, no packages to install.
- STM32CubeProgrammer or STM32CubeIDE (`STM32_Programmer_CLI` is found automatically,
  or pass `--programmer` / set `STM32_PROGRAMMER_CLI`) and an ST-Link on the SWD pins.
- **A firmware built with `CFG_DEBUGGER_SUPPORTED=1`** (CubeMX: STM32_WPAN → Debugger,
  or `Core/Inc/app_conf.h`). Otherwise `APPD_Init` switches PA13/PA14 to analog and
  disables debug in low-power modes, and the probe cannot reach the MCU while it runs
  (the tool reports this after `--swd-timeout`, default 10 s).

## Notes

- The override lives in the GPIO registers: it survives the script exiting and is
  cleared by any reset. Booting with VBUS low cannot be simulated this way, because
  the firmware reconfigures PA2 during start-up.
- Use `--vid` / `--pid` if the USB descriptor changes, `--no-host` when the cable is
  not plugged into the machine running the script, `--sn` with several ST-Links.
- The ST-Link can get stuck when an SWD access is interrupted (libusb timeouts,
  `ST-LINK SN : -`). `reset-probe` resets it at USB level; unplugging it also works.

## BLE trace (`ble_trace.py`)

The BLE controller can refuse a connection without reporting anything to the
application, so some BLE problems cannot be seen from a normal build. `ble_trace.py`
adds a temporary trace to `app_ble.c` and reads it back over SWD while the firmware
runs:

```bash
python ble_trace.py instrument            # edits app_ble.c and app_conf.h in place
#   ... build and flash as usual ...

# FlySight 2 BLE investigation: full conversation

Export of the Claude Code session in which the FlySight 2 BLE problems were investigated
on macOS, Android and iPadOS. It starts with an earlier task of the same session (a CLI that
fakes USB plug/unplug over the ST-Link), which built the bench used later.

- 62 user messages, 198 assistant messages, 1024 tool calls, in chronological order.
- The user writes mostly in French; the assistant answers in French or English.
- Every tool call is shown with its command. Long commands and outputs are shortened; the
  place and the size of each cut are marked. Screenshots are left out.
- The assistant's private reasoning and the application's own system messages are not included.
- Three things are replaced by a placeholder: a Google OAuth client ID, a Wi-Fi network
  name and a calendar entry that appeared in tool output.
- Paths under `/private/tmp/claude-501/.../scratchpad` were temporary files on the Mac.
  The parts worth keeping were committed to the firmware repository as `Scripts/cli/`.

The conclusions are in `ble-pairing-fixes-report.html`, next to this file. Earlier statements
in the conversation were sometimes wrong and corrected later; the report is the reference.

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

This file holds the **rules**: what you must do, and what you must not do. Procedures and
descriptions were moved to `docs/` on 2026-08-27, so that every session does not pay for them.
Open a file below when its trigger applies — not before, and not out of curiosity.

## Reference documents

- **`docs/architecture.md`** — you are looking for where a file belongs, which Gradle name maps to
  which directory, or what depends on what. 28 Gradle modules, the measured dependency graph, and
  the one module whose directory does not match its name.
- **`docs/local-properties.md`** — fresh clone, a build that warns about a missing key, or a
  sign-in screen that refuses to start and names a file you do not have. Four keys, and that is
  the whole list.
- **`docs/testing-usermodule.md`** — you are about to touch `UserModule`, or to run
  `:UserModule:allTests` and wonder why Gradle is downloading the Firebase C++ SDK, or to open a
  ticket about `src/jvmMain/` being covered by nothing. Read it first: that last one is settled.
- **`docs/logging-ci.md`** — the `lint:logging` job turned your pipeline red, or you are about to
  argue that a trace is harmless because it is "only" a `Log.v`.
- **`docs/native-libraries.md`** — you are modifying C/C++ sources, forcing a native rebuild, or
  chasing an `UnsatisfiedLinkError` that names no directory. Holds the `<platform>` / `<ext>` /
  `<jna-prefix>` table and the stale-prefix trap when the build host changes.
- **`docs/cocoapods-ios.md`** — you are raising a Firebase or GoogleSignIn pod version. Two places
  must agree pod by pod, a mismatch crashes at runtime rather than failing the build, and one
  manual pipeline run with `GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS: -ffdx` is not optional.
- **`docs/ble-file-transfer.md`** — you are touching the phone↔Quest chunked file transfer: wire
  format, flow, key parameters and the code locations on both sides.
- **`docs/adb-and-analytics.md`** — you need logs off a headset that is not cabled, or to check
  that an analytics event actually left the device and reached DebugView.

## Development Phase

The project is in active development. Breaking changes are acceptable — there is no need to implement migration systems for new versions (e.g., data format changes, renamed storage paths, schema updates).

## Git Restrictions

**Mutable git commands on the user's request only, for a given block of work.** Commands that read git state (e.g., `git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git branch --list`) are always allowed. A command that changes git state — commit, push, checkout, branch, tag, merge, rebase, and the like — runs only when the user asks for it, and that request covers the block of work it was given for, not the next one.

**Two exceptions, and they are the only mutable git commands you may run on your own:**

```bash
git submodule update --init --recursive
git config core.hooksPath Tools/git-hooks
```

# FlySight 2 BLE Interface Developer Documentation

## Overview

This document describes the Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) interface for the FlySight 2 device. This interface allows applications to interact with the FlySight 2 for file access (reading, writing, deleting files and directories), accessing real-time sensor data, and managing device state.

The interface utilizes standard BLE GATT services where applicable, but primarily relies on custom services for its core functionality. Familiarity with BLE concepts (GATT, Services, Characteristics, UUIDs, Notifications, Writes, Bonding, Security Modes) is recommended.

**Note:** This interface is under active development. Details may change in future firmware versions. This documentation reflects the state based on developer discussions and firmware code (`v2024.11.11.release_candidate` or similar, check `flysight.txt` for exact version).

## Prerequisites

*   **Firmware:** A FlySight 2 unit running firmware version `v2024.11.11.release_candidate` or later is recommended to ensure compatibility with the features described here, especially the pairing mechanism and connection timeout. Firmware updates can be performed via the [online tool](https://flysight.ca/firmware/?include_beta=true). Note that different hardware batches (B1-B5, identifiable via `flysight.txt` or serial number) require specific firmware builds.
*   **BLE Client:** A BLE central device (e.g., smartphone, computer) with a compatible BLE stack and application, supporting secure connections (pairing/bonding) and configurable MTU.

## Core Concepts

### Pairing, Bonding, and Security

FlySight 2 employs BLE security features (bonding and whitelisting) to prevent unauthorized access.

1.  **Pairing Request Mode:**
    *   To initiate pairing with a *new* central device, the FlySight 2 must be put into "Pairing Request Mode".
    *   **Activation:** While the unit is off (Idle Mode, LED is off), perform **two short presses** of the power button.
    *   **Indication:** The **green LED** will pulse slowly (2-second period).
    *   **Advertising:** In this mode, the FlySight advertises as "limited discoverable" and includes specific manufacturer data indicating pairing mode is active (`0xDB0901`, see Advertising section).
    *   **Duration:** Pairing request mode lasts for 30 seconds, or until a BLE connection is established, or until the button is pressed again (which cancels it and returns to Idle).
    *   **Functionality:** While in this mode, *any* central device can connect and initiate pairing/bonding. The whitelist filter is temporarily disabled.

2.  **Whitelisting (Filter Accept List):**
    *   FlySight 2 uses the BLE "filter accept list" (based on the bonded device list). Outside of Pairing Request Mode, it only accepts connections from devices on this list (i.e., devices it has previously bonded with).
    *   **Adding Devices:** When a central device successfully completes the bonding process initiated during Pairing Request Mode, its address/identity is added to the FlySight's internal bonded device list, effectively whitelisting it for future connections.
    *   **Storage:** The bonded device list (including security keys like IRK/ERK) is stored persistently in the FlySight 2's non-volatile memory.
    *   **Reconnecting with an identity address:** Bonded devices are also loaded into the controller's resolving list in *device privacy* mode, so a central may reconnect either from a resolvable private address or from its identity address. macOS connects from its public identity address; in the default *network privacy* mode the controller silently ignores such a request and the central just times out.

3.  **Bonding Process:**
    *   **Initiation:** After connecting to a FlySight 2 in Pairing Request Mode, the central device *must* initiate bonding to establish a secure, encrypted link and be added to the whitelist.
    *   **Security:** FlySight 2 requests **Security Mode 1, Level 2** (Authenticate

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Scan for FlySight 2 adverts through BlueZ (D-Bus) and print each change.

import sys, time

dbus.mainloop.glib.DBusGMainLoop(set_as_default=True)
bus = dbus.SystemBus()
om = dbus.Interface(bus.get_object('org.bluez', '/'), 'org.freedesktop.DBus.ObjectManager')
adapter = dbus.Interface(bus.get_object('org.bluez', '/org/bluez/hci0'), 'org.bluez.Adapter1')
t0 = time.time()
seen = {}

def is_fs(props):
    md = props.get('ManufacturerData', {})
    name = str(props.get('Name', '') or props.get('Alias', ''))
    return 0x09DB in [int(k) for k in md.keys()] or 'FlySight' in name

def show(path, props, why):
    md = props.get('ManufacturerData', {})
    flag = None
    for k, v in md.items():
        if int(k) == 0x09DB:
            flag = ''.join('%02x' % int(b) for b in v)
    key = (str(props.get('Address', '')), flag)
    if seen.get(path) == key and why == 'chg':
        return
    seen[path] = key
    print('%6.1f %s %s type=%s name=%r flag=%s rssi=%s paired=%s bonded=%s connected=%s' % (
        time.time() - t0, why, props.get('Address', '?'), props.get('AddressType', '?'),
        str(props.get('Name', props.get('Alias', ''))), flag, props.get('RSSI', '?'),
        int(props.get('Paired', 0)), int(props.get('Bonded', 0)), int(props.get('Connected', 0))), flush=True)

def added(path, ifaces):
    p = ifaces.get('org.bluez.Device1')
    if p and is_fs(p):
        show(path, p, 'new')

def changed(iface, ch, inv, path=None):
    if iface != 'org.bluez.Device1':
        return
    if not ('ManufacturerData' in ch or 'RSSI' in ch or 'Address' in ch):
        return
    p = dbus.Interface(bus.get_object('org.bluez', path), 'org.freedesktop.DBus.Properties').GetAll('org.bluez.Device1')
    if is_fs(p):
        show(path, p, 'chg' if 'ManufacturerData' not in ch else 'adv')

bus.add_signal_receiver(added, dbus_interface='org.freedesktop.DBus.ObjectManager', signal_name='InterfacesAdded')
bus.add_signal_receiver(changed, dbus_interface='org.freedesktop.DBus.Properties', signal_name='PropertiesChanged', path_keyword='path')
for path, ifaces in om.GetManagedObjects().items():
    added(path, ifaces)
adapter.SetDiscoveryFilter({'Transport': 'le', 'DuplicateData': True})
adapter.StartDiscovery()
loop = GLib.MainLoop()
GLib.timeout_add(int(DUR * 1000), loop.quit)
loop.run()
try:
    adapter.StopDiscovery()
except Exception:
    pass
print('scan done, %d FlySight object(s)' % len(seen))
EOF
python3 scan.py 12

# Native libraries (C/C++)

> Moved out of `CLAUDE.md` on 2026-08-27, verbatim. **Platform values** was a sibling section of
> **CocoaPods** there; it is folded in here because the `<platform>`, `<ext>` and `<jna-prefix>`
> placeholders it resolves are only ever used by the three build recipes above it. Open this file
> when you modify C/C++ sources, or when you are chasing an `UnsatisfiedLinkError` that names no
> directory.

The project uses native C/C++ libraries with automatic rebuild detection via Gradle's input hashing. Gradle tracks the hash of all source files — if any `.c`, `.cpp`, `.h`, `.m`, `.cmake`, `CMakeLists.txt`, or `build.sh` changes, the native library is automatically rebuilt. If nothing changed, the task is `UP-TO-DATE` (skipped).

## Firebase Native Library (`UserModule`)

- **Source:** `Modules/Feature/UserModule/src/nativeInterop/c/`
- **Build config:** `Modules/Feature/UserModule/src/nativeInterop/CMakeLists.txt`, `cmake/*.cmake`, `build.sh`
- **Build output:** `Modules/Feature/UserModule/src/nativeInterop/build/<platform>/libskygames_firebase.<ext>`
- **Resource output:** `Modules/Feature/UserModule/src/jvmMain/resources/<jna-prefix>/libskygames_firebase.<ext>`

Rebuild is automatic when sources change. To force a rebuild manually:
```bash
rm -f Modules/Feature/UserModule/src/nativeInterop/build/<platform>/libskygames_firebase.<ext>
./gradlew :UserModule:buildNativeFirebaseLib
```

## Text-to-speech Native Library (`AudioModule`)

- **Source:** `Modules/MiddleWare/AudioModule/src/nativeInterop/c/` (wraps eSpeak-ng)
- **Build output:** `Modules/MiddleWare/AudioModule/src/nativeInterop/build/<platform>/libskygames_tts.<ext>`
- **Resource output:** `Modules/MiddleWare/AudioModule/src/jvmMain/resources/<jna-prefix>/libskygames_tts.<ext>`

The compiled voice data goes to `src/jvmMain/resources/espeak-ng-data/`, which carries no
[... 54 lines omitted ...]

This was measured rather than assumed, because the shape of the tasks suggests otherwise and the
wrong guess is the expensive one. `UserModule` and `AudioModule` declare a single file as their
output, so nothing else in the directory is theirs to clean. `FlySightApi/core` declares the whole
resources directory as an `@OutputDirectory`, which looks as though Gradle would clean it — it does
not. Building it once under a foreign prefix and then normally leaves both directories side by
side. Note also that CI keeps ignored files between pipelines (`GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS: -ffd`), so a stale
directory outlives a pipeline too.

**Only the two 64-bit architectures are accepted**, and anything else makes the copy task fail with
an explicit message rather than guess a prefix. This errs on the side of stopping rather than
enumerating architectures nobody builds on here; note in passing that 32-bit ARM could not be
derived anyway, being `linux-arm` or `linux-armel` according to a runtime soft-float test a build

- Services automatically discovered by BlueZ after connection
- Accessed via `GetManagedObjects` on object manager interface

#### Read Characteristic (`ble_read_characteristic`)
1. Finds characteristic D-Bus path by UUID
2. Calls `ReadValue` method on characteristic interface
3. Returns data via callback (synchronous in current implementation)

#### Write Characteristic (`ble_write_characteristic`)

2. Calls `WriteValue` with byte array
3. Supports both write-with-response and write-without-response
4. Invokes callback on completion

#### Notifications (`ble_enable_notifications`, `ble_disable_notifications`)
- **Enable**: Calls `StartNotify` on characteristic
  - Stores callback for future notifications
  - Notifications delivered via `PropertiesChanged` signals

- **Disable**: Calls `StopNotify`
  - Removes callback registration

### Thread Safety
- All public API functions protected by pthread mutex
- D-Bus signals processed in separate GLib event loop thread
- Callbacks invoked from signal handler thread (application must handle synchronization)

## D-Bus Object Hierarchy

```
/org/bluez
├── /org/bluez/hci0                           (Adapter)
│   ├── /org/bluez/hci0/dev_XX_XX_XX_XX_XX_XX (Device)
│   │   ├── /org/bluez/hci0/dev_.../service0000 (Service)
│   │   │   ├── /org/bluez/hci0/dev_.../service0000/char0001 (Characteristic)
│   │   │   │   └── /org/bluez/hci0/dev_.../service0000/char0001/desc0001 (Descriptor)
```

## BlueZ D-Bus Interfaces Used

| Interface | Methods | Signals |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `org.bluez.Adapter1` | `StartDiscovery`, `StopDiscovery` | - |
| `org.bluez.Device1` | `Connect`, `Disconnect` | - |
| `org.bluez.GattCharacteristic1` | `ReadValue`, `WriteValue`, `StartNotify`, `StopNotify` | - |
| `org.freedesktop.DBus.ObjectManager` | `GetManagedObjects` | `InterfacesAdded`, `InterfacesRemoved` |
| `org.freedesktop.DBus.Properties` | `Get`, `Set` | `PropertiesChanged` |

## Error Handling

All functions return error codes defined in `flysight_ble.h`:
- `BLE_SUCCESS` (0) - Operation successful
- `BLE_ERROR_INIT_FAILED` (-1) - D-Bus connection or adapter not found

    // didUpdateValueForCharacteristic. A strong reference must be kept for the whole

        if (result != FlySightBleNative.BLE_SUCCESS) {
            val errorMsg = FlySightBleNative.INSTANCE.ble_get_error_string(result)

package ca.flysight.internal.bluetooth

import ca.flysight.api.core.internal.bluetooth.BleDeviceSocket
import ca.flysight.api.core.internal.socket.DeviceSocket
import ca.flysight.api.core.model.FlySightInfo
import ca.flysight.api.core.tools.log.FlySightLogger
import ca.flysight.api.core.tools.log.LoggerCombiner
import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope
import kotlinx.coroutines.delay
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.channelFlow
import kotlinx.coroutines.launch

class DefaultBluetoothService(
    private val delegate: BluetoothServiceDelegate
) : BluetoothService {

    /**
     * flysightble-style escalation around the lifecycle-bound delegate scan:
     * scan for [SCAN_PHASES_MS]\[0] ms; if still no device, extend by the next phase;
     * stop as soon as at least one device was seen at a checkpoint, or once all phases
     * are exhausted.
     */
    override fun scan(): Flow<List<BluetoothDeviceInfo>> = channelFlow {
        var latest: List<BluetoothDeviceInfo> = emptyList()
        val job = launch {
            delegate.scan().collect { snapshot ->
                latest = snapshot
                send(snapshot)
            }
        }
        for (phase in SCAN_PHASES_MS) {
            delay(phase)
            if (latest.isNotEmpty()) {
                break
            }
        }
        job.cancel()
        close()
    }

    companion object {
        private val SCAN_PHASES_MS = longArrayOf(10_000L, 10_000L, 20_000L)
    }

    override fun createBluetoothSocket(info: FlySightInfo, scope: CoroutineScope, logger: FlySightLogger): DeviceSocket? {
        val socketDelegate = delegate.createBluetoothSocketDelegate(info, scope, logger) ?: return null
        val policy = delegate.platformPolicyPick
        val deviceSocket = BleDeviceSocket(
            id = info.id,
            scope = scope,
            delegate = socketDelegate,
            policy = policy,
            logger = logger
        )
        return deviceSocket
    }

package ca.flysight.api.core.internal.bluetooth

@OptIn(ExperimentalUuidApi::class)
sealed class FlySightCharacteristic(val name: String, val uuid: Uuid) {
    data object CRS_RX : FlySightCharacteristic("CRS_RX", CRS_RX_UUID)
    data object CRS_TX : FlySightCharacteristic("CRS_TX", CRS_TX_UUID)
    data object GNSS_PV : FlySightCharacteristic("GNSS_PV", GNSS_PV_UUID)
    data object START_CONTROL : FlySightCharacteristic("START_CONTROL", START_CONTROL_UUID)
    data object START_RESULT : FlySightCharacteristic("START_RESULT", START_RESULT_UUID)
    data object MODE : FlySightCharacteristic("MODE", MODE_UUID)
    data object GNSS_CONTROL : FlySightCharacteristic("GNSS_CONTROL", GNSS_CONTROL_UUID)
    data object BATTERY : FlySightCharacteristic("BATTERY", batteryLevelCharUuid)
    companion object {
        fun values(): List<FlySightCharacteristic> {
            return listOf(
                CRS_TX,
                CRS_RX,
                GNSS_PV,
                START_CONTROL,
                START_RESULT,
                MODE,
                GNSS_CONTROL,
                BATTERY
            )
        }

        fun fromUuid(uuid: Uuid?): FlySightCharacteristic? {
            return when (uuid) {
                CRS_RX_UUID -> CRS_RX
                CRS_TX_UUID -> CRS_TX
                GNSS_PV_UUID -> GNSS_PV
                START_CONTROL_UUID -> START_CONTROL
                START_RESULT_UUID -> START_RESULT
                MODE_UUID -> MODE
                GNSS_CONTROL_UUID -> GNSS_CONTROL
                batteryLevelCharUuid -> BATTERY
                else -> null
            }
        }
    }
}

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Simulate plugging / unplugging the USB cable of a FlySight 2 over SWD (ST-Link).

The USB cable stays physically connected. The firmware decides that USB power
is present from one GPIO, PA2 (VBUS_DIV), an input with an interrupt on both
edges (see FlySight/vbus.c and FlySight/mode.c). This tool takes over that pin:

  unplug  drives PA2 low (pin switched to output)
          -> firmware sees VBUS_LOW, leaves USB mode, stops the USB peripheral,
             the host sees the device disappear.
  plug    gives PA2 back (pin switched to input)
          -> the real VBUS level returns, the EXTI fires on the rising edge,
             firmware enters USB mode and the host enumerates it again.

The firmware runs exactly the code path of a real unplug/plug (EXTI2 ->
FS_VBUS_Triggered -> mode state machine); it needs no test hook. The override
lives in the MCU's GPIO registers, so it survives this script exiting and is
cleared by any reset.

Requires STM32_Programmer_CLI (STM32CubeProgrammer, also bundled with
STM32CubeIDE). SWD access is HOTPLUG: the core is never halted.

Usage:
    python vbus.py status
    python vbus.py unplug
    python vbus.py plug
    python vbus.py cycle -n 20 --off 2 --on 3
    python vbus.py reset
"""

import argparse
import ctypes
import ctypes.util
import glob
import os
import re
import shutil
import signal
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass

# VBUS_DIV is PA2 (Core/Inc/main.h)
GPIOA = 0x48000000
GPIOA_MODER = GPIOA + 0x00
GPIOA_IDR = GPIOA + 0x10
GPIOA_ODR = GPIOA + 0x14
GPIOA_BSRR = GPIOA + 0x18
VBUS_PIN = 2
VBUS_BIT = 1 << VBUS_PIN
GPIOC = 0x48000800
BUTTON_PIN = 12                       # BUTTON_Pin on GPIOC, pressed when low
MODER_MASK = 0b11 << (2 * VBUS_PIN)   # PA0..PA3 live in byte 0 of MODER
MODER_OUTPUT = 0b01 << (2 * VBUS_PIN)

# Used to check from the MCU side that the firmware reacted
RCC_APB1ENR1 = 0x58000058
RCC_APB1ENR1_USBEN = 1 << 26
USB_BCDR = 0x40006858
USB_BCDR_DPPU = 1 << 15               # D+ pull-up: device is attached to the bus

SCB_CFSR = 0xE000ED28
SCB_HFSR = 0xE000ED2C

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# dev.sh — runs this project on this Mac: the development environment. It takes no argument and
# asks nothing.
#
#   ./dev.sh
#
# It starts, with Podman, the pod deploy.sh puts on the server: one container per folder that holds
# a Containerfile, built from the very same files. What differs is where it runs and what it holds:
# its own database, its own secrets, and no public name — the phones of the local network reach it
# at the address of this Mac, in plain HTTP (http://192.168.1.x:<port>). Nothing of it touches the
# server, and the server knows nothing of it.
#
# What it reads in a Containerfile is what deploy.sh reads (see its header), and one thing more:
#
#   LABEL dev.env.NAME="value"    an environment variable given to the container here, in place of
#                                 the one its ENV line gives it on the server. HOST in the value
#                                 is replaced by the address of this Mac on the local network.
#
# The secrets: the ones drawn at random on the server are drawn at random here too, once, other
# values; the ones read in local.properties are the same lines (deploy.NAME=…). Podman keeps them,
# next to the data, in its own machine: neither is written in the project.
#
# Running it again rebuilds what changed and restarts the pod; the data stays. To stop the pod:
#   podman pod stop <project>-dev
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"     # the root of the project

SECRETS_FILE=local.properties   # where the values of the secrets are read
HEALTH_WAIT=300                 # seconds given to the pod to answer; the database's first start is the long one

die() { echo "✗ $*" >&2; exit 1; }
step() { echo; echo "── $*"; }
# One value of one container, kept in a variable named after both.
set_c() { printf -v "C_$1_$2" '%s' "$3"; }
get_c() { local v="C_$1_$2"; echo "${!v:-}"; }
# What a Containerfile declares.
label() { sed -nE "s/^LABEL[[:space:]]+deploy\.$2=\"(.*)\"[[:space:]]*\$/\1/p" "$1" | head -1; }                    # one value
labels() { sed -nE "s/^LABEL[[:space:]]+deploy\.$2\.([A-Za-z0-9._-]+)=\".*\"[[:space:]]*\$/\1/p" "$1" | tr '\n' ' '; }   # the names of one kind of secret
dev_env() { sed -nE "s/^LABEL[[:space:]]+dev\.env\.([A-Za-z0-9_]+)=\"(.*)\"[[:space:]]*\$/\1=\2/p" "$1"; }          # NAME=value, one per line
# The value of a secret, in local.properties.
secret_value() {
  [ -f "$SECRETS_FILE" ] || return 0
  local key; key="$(printf '%s' "$1" | sed 's/[.[\*^$]/\\&/g')"
  sed -n "s/^deploy\.$key=//p" "$SECRETS_FILE" | head -1
}

import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.update
import kotlinx.coroutines.launch

class DefaultFlySightService(
    private val flySightApi: FlySightApi,
    private val permissionService: PermissionService,
    private val lightStorageService: LightStorageService,
    private val dialogService: DialogService
) : FlySightService {

    private val _knownDevices = MutableStateFlow<List<FlySightDevice>>(emptyList())
    override val knownDevices: StateFlow<List<FlySightDevice>> = _knownDevices.asStateFlow()

    private val _selectedDevice = MutableStateFlow<FlySightDevice?>(null)
    override val selectedDevice: StateFlow<FlySightDevice?> = _selectedDevice.asStateFlow()

    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + CoroutineName("FlySightService_scope") + Dispatchers.IO)


    private var reconstructed = false

    init {
        // Known devices can only be rebuilt once the BLE stack is ready: on iOS
        // a persisted device is reconstructed via the shared CBCentralManager,
        // which returns nothing until it is poweredOn. Reacting to the shared
        // bluetooth state (instead of reconstructing synchronously at startup)
        // guarantees the central is usable when createDevice runs.
        scope.launch {
            permissionService.bluetoothState.collect { state ->
                if (state == BluetoothState.Enabled && !reconstructed) {
                    reconstructed = true
                    reconstructKnownDevices()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    private fun reconstructKnownDevices() {
        val storedInfos = deserializeDeviceList(lightStorageService.observe(KEY_KNOWN_DEVICES).value)
        val devices = storedInfos.mapNotNull { flySightApi.createDevice(it) }
        _knownDevices.value = devices
        val selectedId = lightStorageService.observe(KEY_SELECTED_DEVICE_ID).value
        _selectedDevice.value = devices.find { it.id == selectedId }
        // Known device: reconnect without scanning — on desktop createDevice/connect re-resolves
        // it via retrievePeripheralsWithIdentifiers. New devices go through the scan dialog.
        _selectedDevice.value?.let { device ->
            scope.launch {
                device.connect()
            }
        }
    }

        if (!ensureBluetoothReady()) {
            return
        }

                knownDeviceIds = { _knownDevices.value.map { it.id }.toSet() },
                onDeviceSelected = { device ->
                    addDevice(device)
                    scope.launch {
                        connectToDevice(device)

**Tool: Bash** — Test whether registering a BlueZ agent switches the adapter to bondable

~~~~bash
cd "[scratchpad]/blelab" && cat > agent_probe.py <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Does registering a BlueZ agent change the adapter's Pairable (kernel "bondable") setting?"""
import time
import dbus, dbus.service, dbus.mainloop.glib
from gi.repository import GLib

dbus.mainloop.glib.DBusGMainLoop(set_as_default=True)
bus = dbus.SystemBus()
props = dbus.Interface(bus.get_object('org.bluez', '/org/bluez/hci0'), 'org.freedesktop.DBus.Properties')
mgr = dbus.Interface(bus.get_object('org.bluez', '/org/bluez'), 'org.bluez.AgentManager1')
PATH = '/fr/hozakan/probe/agent'

class Agent(dbus.service.Object):
    @dbus.service.method('org.bluez.Agent1', in_signature='', out_signature='')
    def Release(self):
        print('agent: Release')

agent = Agent(bus, PATH)
ctx = GLib.MainLoop().get_context()

def pump(sec=0.6):
    end = time.time() + sec
    while time.time() < end:
        ctx.iteration(False)
        time.sleep(0.02)

def pairable(label):
    pump()
    print('%-44s Pairable=%s' % (label, bool(props.Get('org.bluez.Adapter1', 'Pairable'))))

pairable('before')
mgr.RegisterAgent(PATH, 'NoInputNoOutput')
pairable('after RegisterAgent (not default)')
mgr.RequestDefaultAgent(PATH)
pairable('after RequestDefaultAgent')
mgr.UnregisterAgent(PATH)
pairable('after UnregisterAgent')
EOF
python3 agent_probe.py; grep -n "Pairable\|Privacy\|JustWorks\|Temporary" /etc/bluetooth/main.conf | head -20
~~~~

Je la réécris en suivant le contrat de [ble_macos.m](/home/[user]/AndroidStudioProjects/skygames/Libs/FlySightApi/core/src/nativeInterop/c/macos/ble_macos.m).

abstract class BuildNativeLibTask : Exec() {
    @get:InputDirectory
    abstract val nativeInteropDir: DirectoryProperty
    
    init {
        val osName = System.getProperty("os.name").lowercase(Locale.getDefault())
        if (osName.contains("windows")) {
            commandLine("cmd", "/c", "build.bat")
        } else {
            commandLine("bash", "build.sh")
        }
    }
    
    @TaskAction
    override fun exec() {
        workingDir = nativeInteropDir.get().asFile
        
        val osName = System.getProperty("os.name").lowercase(Locale.getDefault())
        val platform = when {
            osName.contains("mac") || osName.contains("darwin") -> "macos"
            osName.contains("linux") -> "linux"
            osName.contains("windows") -> "windows"
            else -> throw GradleException("Unsupported platform: $osName")
        }
        
        val platformBuildDir = nativeInteropDir.get().asFile.resolve("build/$platform")
        platformBuildDir.mkdirs()
        
        super.exec()
    }
}

def ioreg_has_device(text, vid, pid):
    for block in re.split(r"(?m)^[\s|]*\+-o ", text):
        if re.search(rf'"idVendor" = {vid}\b', block) and re.search(rf'"idProduct" = {pid}\b', block):
            return True
    return False


def wait_for(predicate, timeout, interval=0.05):
    """Seconds until predicate() is true, or None on timeout."""
    start = time.monotonic()
    while True:
        if predicate():
            return time.monotonic() - start
        if time.monotonic() - start >= timeout:
            return None
        time.sleep(interval)


class Bench:
    """What the tests look at: the MCU's reaction, and optionally the host's."""

    def __init__(self, swd, vid, pid, check_host):
        self.swd = swd
        self.vid = vid
        self.pid = pid
        self.check_host = check_host

    def wait_firmware(self, active, timeout):
        return wait_for(lambda: read_state(self.swd).usb_active == active, timeout)

    def wait_host(self, present, timeout):
        return wait_for(lambda: host_has_device(self.vid, self.pid) == present, timeout)


def fmt_time(t):
    return "TIMEOUT" if t is None else f"{t:.2f}s"


def explain_failure(swd):
    """Say why the firmware may not have reacted."""
    st = read_state(swd)
    if st.faulted:
        print(f"  firmware has faulted since the last clear: {st.fault_text()} "
              f"(CFSR=0x{st.cfsr:08X} HFSR=0x{st.hfsr:08X}); a crashed firmware cannot react")


def make_bench(swd, args):
    check_host = not args.no_host
    if check_host and host_has_device(args.vid, args.pid) is None:
        print("note: host-side USB check not supported on this platform", file=sys.stderr)
        check_host = False
    return Bench(swd, args.vid, args.pid, check_host)


def cmd_status(swd, args):
    st = read_state(swd)
    print(f"VBUS_DIV (PA2)   : {'HIGH' if st.pin_high else 'LOW'}"
          f"  ({'FORCED by this tool' if st.forced else 'following the real VBUS'})")
    print(f"firmware USB     : {'active (clock on, D+ pull-up on)' if st.usb_active else 'off'}")
    host = host_has_device(args.vid, args.pid)
    if host is not None:
        print(f"host sees USB    : {'yes' if host else 'no'}  ({args.vid:04x}:{args.pid:04x})")
    if st.faulted:
        print(f"fault flags      : {st.fault_text()}  "
              f"(CFSR=0x{st.cfsr:08X} HFSR=0x{st.hfsr:08X}; sticky, see --clear-faults)")

def _terminate(signum, frame):
    # Same path as Ctrl-C, so cycle's `finally` still gives PA2 back
    raise KeyboardInterrupt


def main(argv=None):
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, _terminate)
    try:
        swd = Swd(find_programmer(args.programmer), sn=args.sn, timeout=args.swd_timeout)
        return args.func(swd, args)
    except SwdError as e:
        print(f"error: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("\ninterrupted", file=sys.stderr)
        return 130


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Record what the BLE stack reports to the firmware, and read it back over SWD.

The BLE controller can refuse a connection without telling the application
(see "Reconnecting with an identity address" in Docs/ble.md). To see that from
the FlySight side, this tool adds a temporary trace to app_ble.c:

  - a ring of the last 64 events in RAM: every advertising start (pairing mode
    or not, addresses in use), connection, disconnection, encryption change and
    GAP event;
  - two RAM switches that turn a fix off and on again without reflashing, so
    one boot and one bond can be compared with and without it:
      privacy  Device Privacy mode for bonded peers (ble_count_bonded_devices)
      window   request_pairing cleared in Adv_Update

The trace is test code. `instrument` edits the sources in place, `restore`
removes it again; it is never meant to be committed. It also sets
CFG_DEBUGGER_SUPPORTED to 1, which SWD access to a running firmware needs.

Usage:
    python ble_trace.py instrument          # then build and flash as usual
    python ble_trace.py read --elf build.elf
    python ble_trace.py mark --elf build.elf
    python ble_trace.py read --elf build.elf --since 12
    python ble_trace.py set privacy off --elf build.elf
    python ble_trace.py restore

The ELF must be the one that is running: the addresses of the trace come from
its symbol table. FLYSIGHT_ELF can be set instead of passing --elf.
"""

import argparse
import os
import re
import struct
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
from vbus import Swd, SwdError, find_programmer  # noqa: E402

REPO = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))
APP_BLE = "STM32_WPAN/App/app_ble.c"
APP_CONF = "Core/Inc/app_conf.h"
MARKER = "TEMP-BLE-TRACE"

RECORDS = 64
RECORD_SIZE = 32
SWITCHES = {"privacy": "ble_trace_fix_privacy", "window": "ble_trace_fix_window"}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Instrumentation: (file, text to find, text to put instead). Each text to find
# must occur exactly once, so a change in the firmware that breaks an anchor is
# reported instead of producing a half-instrumented build.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

PATCHES = [
    (APP_CONF,
     "#define CFG_DEBUGGER_SUPPORTED    0\n",
     "#define CFG_DEBUGGER_SUPPORTED    1 /* TEMP-BLE-TRACE */\n"),
    for path, text in contents.items():
        with open(os.path.join(root, path), "w", newline="") as f:
            f.write(text)
    return sorted(contents)

def test_forced(self):
        self.assertFalse(self.state().forced)
        self.assertTrue(self.state(moder=0x6ABFFBDF).forced)

    def test_usb_active_needs_clock_and_pullup(self):
        usben = 1 << 26
        self.assertTrue(self.state(apb1enr1=usben, bcdr=1 << 15).usb_active)
        self.assertFalse(self.state(apb1enr1=0, bcdr=1 << 15).usb_active)
        self.assertFalse(self.state(apb1enr1=usben, bcdr=0).usb_active)

    def test_fault_text(self):
        st = self.state(cfsr=1 << 17, hfsr=1 << 30)
        self.assertTrue(st.faulted)
        self.assertEqual(st.fault_text(), "HardFault(forced) INVSTATE")
        self.assertFalse(self.state().faulted)


class SwdTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def swd(self, stdout, stderr=""):
        def runner(args, **kw):
            self.args = args
            return types.SimpleNamespace(stdout=stdout, stderr=stderr)
        return Swd("/x/STM32_Programmer_CLI", sn="ABC", runner=runner)

    def test_read_parses_values_and_strips_colors(self):
        out = ("\x1b[39;49m\x1b[0mReading 32-bit memory content\n"
               "0x48000000 : 6ABFFBCF\n0x48000010 : 00008024\n")
        swd = self.swd(out)
        self.assertEqual(swd.read((0x48000000, 32), (0x48000010, 32)), [0x6ABFFBCF, 0x8024])
        self.assertIn("mode=HOTPLUG", self.args)
        self.assertIn("sn=ABC", self.args)
        self.assertEqual(self.args[self.args.index("-r32") + 1:self.args.index("-r32") + 3],
                         ["0x48000000", "4"])

    def test_read_byte(self):
        swd = self.swd("0x48000000 : CF\n")
        self.assertEqual(swd.read((0x48000000, 8)), [0xCF])
        self.assertIn("-r8", self.args)

    def test_read_reports_programmer_error(self):
        swd = self.swd("Error: No STM32 target found!\n")
        with self.assertRaisesRegex(SwdError, "No STM32 target"):
            swd.read((0x48000000, 32))

    def test_hung_probe_gives_actionable_error(self):
        import subprocess

        def runner(args, **kw):
            raise subprocess.TimeoutExpired(args, kw["timeout"])
        swd = Swd("/x/STM32_Programmer_CLI", timeout=1, runner=runner)
        with self.assertRaisesRegex(SwdError, "CFG_DEBUGGER_SUPPORTED"):
            swd.read((0x48000000, 32))

    def test_write8_checks_status(self):
        self.swd("Downloading 8-bit data done successfully\n").write8(0x48000000, 0xDF)
        with self.assertRaises(SwdError):
            self.swd("Downloading 8-bit data failed...\n").write8(0x48000000, 0xDF)

    def test_write32_error_can_be_ignored(self):
        out = "Error: Failed to download data! If it's a Flash memory\n"
        self.swd(out).write32(0x48000018, 1 << 18, check=False)
        with self.assertRaises(SwdError):
            self.swd(out).write32(0x48000018, 1 << 18)

class FakeGpioA:
    """Just enough of GPIOA for PA2: input follows VBUS, output follows ODR."""

    def __init__(self, vbus_present=True, moder=0x6ABFFBCF, odr=0x8000):
        self.vbus_present = vbus_present
        self.moder = moder
        self.odr = odr
        self.stuck_high = False
        self.writes = []

    def idr(self):
        out = (self.moder & MODER_MASK) == MODER_OUTPUT
        high = (self.odr & VBUS_BIT) != 0 if out else self.vbus_present
        if out and self.stuck_high:
            high = True
        return (0x8020 & ~VBUS_BIT) | (VBUS_BIT if high else 0)

    def read(self, *specs):
        values = []
        for addr, width in specs:
            word = {GPIOA_MODER: self.moder, GPIOA_IDR: self.idr(), GPIOA_ODR: self.odr}[addr]
            values.append(word & 0xFF if width == 8 else word)
        return values

    def write8(self, addr, value):
        assert addr == GPIOA_MODER
        self.writes.append(("w8", addr, value))
        self.moder = (self.moder & ~0xFF) | value

    def write32(self, addr, value, check=True):
        assert addr == GPIOA_BSRR
        self.writes.append(("w32", addr, value))
        self.odr = (self.odr | (value & 0xFFFF)) & ~(value >> 16)


class ForceTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_unplug_drives_pa2_low_and_keeps_other_pins(self):
        gpio = FakeGpioA()
        vbus.force_unplugged(gpio)
        self.assertEqual(gpio.moder & MODER_MASK, MODER_OUTPUT)
        self.assertEqual(gpio.moder & ~MODER_MASK, 0x6ABFFBCF & ~MODER_MASK)
        self.assertFalse(gpio.idr() & VBUS_BIT)

    def test_release_restores_input(self):
        gpio = FakeGpioA()
        vbus.force_unplugged(gpio)
        vbus.release_vbus(gpio)
        self.assertEqual(gpio.moder, 0x6ABFFBCF)
        self.assertTrue(gpio.idr() & VBUS_BIT)

    def test_release_follows_real_vbus(self):
        gpio = FakeGpioA(vbus_present=False)
        vbus.force_unplugged(gpio)
        vbus.release_vbus(gpio)
        self.assertFalse(gpio.idr() & VBUS_BIT)

    def test_moder_is_written_one_byte_only(self):
        gpio = FakeGpioA()
        vbus.force_unplugged(gpio)
        vbus.release_vbus(gpio)

~~~~
class FakeGpioC:
    """GPIOC for PC12: a button that pulls the pin low when pressed, otherwise the pull-up wins."""

    GPIOC = vbus.GPIOC

    def __init__(self, moder=0xFFFFFFFF, odr=0x1000):
        self.moder = moder          # reset value of GPIOC.MODER: every pin an input
        self.odr = odr
        self.writes = []

    def idr(self):
        bit = 1 << vbus.BUTTON_PIN
        out = (self.moder >> (2 * vbus.BUTTON_PIN)) & 0b11 == 0b01
        high = (self.odr & bit) != 0 if out else True
        return bit if high else 0

    def _word(self, addr):
        return {self.GPIOC: self.moder, self.GPIOC + 0x10: self.idr(), self.GPIOC + 0x14: self.odr}[addr]

    def read(self, *specs):
        values = []
        for addr, width in specs:
            if width == 8:
                base = addr & ~3
                values.append((self.moder >> (8 * (addr - base))) & 0xFF)
            else:
                values.append(self._word(addr))
        return values

    def write8(self, addr, value):
        shift = 8 * (addr - self.GPIOC)
        self.writes.append(("w8", addr, value))
        self.moder = (self.moder & ~(0xFF << shift)) | (value << shift)

    def write32(self, addr, value, check=True):
        assert addr == self.GPIOC + 0x18
        self.writes.append(("w32", addr, value))
        self.odr = (self.odr | (value & 0xFFFF)) & ~(value >> 16)


class ButtonTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_press_pulls_pc12_low_and_leaves_other_pins(self):

        self.assertFalse(gpio.idr())
        self.assertEqual(gpio.moder & ~(0b11 << 24), 0xABFFFFFF & ~(0b11 << 24))

    def test_release_gives_the_pin_back(self):

        vbus.press_button(gpio)
        vbus.release_button(gpio)
        self.assertEqual(gpio.moder, 0xABFFFFFF & ~(0b11 << 24))
        self.assertTrue(gpio.idr())

        self.assertIn(("w32", vbus.GPIOC + 0x18, (1 << vbus.BUTTON_PIN) << 16), gpio.writes)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Baseline BLE probe for a FlySight 2, straight on BlueZ (D-Bus), without the SkyGames library.

    bluez_probe.py connect [--name FlySight] [--flag 00|01] [--agent] [--pair] [--scan 20]
                           [--no-read] [--hold 0] [--address AA:BB:..]
    bluez_probe.py status  [--name FlySight]
    bluez_probe.py forget  [--name FlySight]

`connect` scans until the FlySight advertises (optionally with a given pairing flag), connects,
reads FT_Packet_In (which needs an encrypted link, so it triggers pairing on a host that is not
bonded), prints what happened and disconnects. Exit code 0 only if the read succeeded.

        ctx.iteration(False)
        time.sleep(0.01)
    return predicate()

**Tool: Write** `/home/[user]/AndroidStudioProjects/skygames/Libs/FlySightApi/core/src/nativeInterop/c/linux/ble_linux.c`

~~~~
/*
 * BLE central for Linux, on top of the BlueZ D-Bus API (through GDBus).
 *
 * Everything that touches BlueZ, and every callback given back to the caller, runs on one
 * worker thread that owns a GLib main context. The functions of the C API hand their work to
 * that thread and wait for it, so the state below needs no lock and the caller gets its
 * callbacks from a single thread, in the order things happened.
 *
 * Three things are specific to BlueZ:
 *
 *  - An agent must be registered. Without one, BlueZ keeps the adapter non-bondable and refuses
 *    the "Just Works" pairing a FlySight uses (the kernel asks user space to confirm it, and
 *    there is nobody to answer). ble_init() registers one, and ble_connect() pairs explicitly
 *    with a device that is not paired yet instead of waiting for the first encrypted request.
 *
 *  - The address of a device changes when it gets paired. A FlySight advertises from a
 *    resolvable private address; once bonded, BlueZ replaces it by the identity address. The
 *    caller keeps the address it saw during the scan, so that first address stays valid as an
 *    identifier: the pair (first address, identity address) is kept in a small file and used in
 *    both directions, for ble_connect() and for the scan results.
 *
 *  - BlueZ keeps the Battery Service for itself and publishes org.bluez.Battery1 instead. It
 *    is given back to the caller as the service and characteristic it replaces.
 */
#include "../include/flysight_ble.h"

#include <gio/gio.h>
#include <glib.h>
#include <glib/gstdio.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

#define BLUEZ_SERVICE "org.bluez"
#define ADAPTER_IFACE "org.bluez.Adapter1"
#define DEVICE_IFACE "org.bluez.Device1"
#define GATT_SERVICE_IFACE "org.bluez.GattService1"
#define GATT_CHAR_IFACE "org.bluez.GattCharacteristic1"
#define BATTERY_IFACE "org.bluez.Battery1"
#define AGENT_MANAGER_IFACE "org.bluez.AgentManager1"
#define AGENT_PATH "/ca/flysight/ble/agent"

#define BATTERY_SERVICE_UUID "0000180f-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb"
#define BATTERY_LEVEL_UUID "00002a19-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb"

#define CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS 30000
#define PAIR_TIMEOUT_MS 30000
#define DISCOVERY_TIMEOUT_MS 10000
#define DISCONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS 5000
#define GATT_TIMEOUT_MS 35000
#define CALL_TIMEOUT_MS 5000
#define SCAN_REPORT_INTERVAL_US G_USEC_PER_SEC
#define MAX_ALIASES 64

/* Bits of the GATT characteristic properties, as the caller expects them */
#define PROPERTY_BROADCAST 0x01
#define PROPERTY_READ 0x02
#define PROPERTY_WRITE_NO_RESPONSE 0x04
#define PROPERTY_WRITE 0x08
#define PROPERTY_NOTIFY 0x10
#define PROPERTY_INDICATE 0x20
#define PROPERTY_SIGNED_WRITE 0x40
#define PROPERTY_EXTENDED 0x80

#define LOG(...) do { fprintf(stderr, "[BLE] " __VA_ARGS__); fputc('\n', stderr); } while (0)

[... 2012 lines omitted ...]

                       void* user_data) {

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Drive libflysight_ble.so (the native BLE layer of SkyGames' FlySightApi) the way the app does.

    fs_probe.py scan [--seconds 10]
    fs_probe.py connect [--name FlySight] [--flag 00|01] [--id ADDRESS] [--stay 0] [--scan 20]

`connect` scans for the FlySight (or takes `--id`, an identifier from an earlier scan, with no
scan at all, as the app does when it starts), connects, discovers the services, subscribes to
the notifications the app subscribes to, reads FT_Packet_In (needs an encrypted link) and sends
a ping, which the FlySight acknowledges with a notification. Exit code 0 only if all of it worked.
"""

# Architecture

> Moved out of `CLAUDE.md` on 2026-08-27 and **rewritten**, because the version that lived there
> was measurably out of date: it showed 8 Gradle modules where `settings.gradle.kts` declares 28,
> it placed `QuestApiModule` under `Modules/MiddleWare/` where it actually lives in `Libs/QuestApi`,
> it gave `composeApp` 5 project dependencies where the build file declares 22, it reduced
> `XRApp` to `MetaProtocolModule` alone where the build file declares five, and it described
> `CoreModule` as holding « shared datetime utils », which nothing here reproduces. Everything
> below was read out of `settings.gradle.kts` and the `build.gradle.kts` files on that date, with
> file:line given so the next reader can re-check rather than trust.
>
> Open this file when you are looking for where a file belongs, or for what depends on what.
> Nothing here is a rule — the rules are in `CLAUDE.md`.

Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) project targeting **Android**, **iOS**, and **Desktop (JVM)** with
Compose Multiplatform UI. The Quest 3 XR app (`XRApp`) is Android-only.

## Folder structure

```
SkyGames/
├── Apps/
│   ├── androidApp/                  (the Android application around composeApp — manifest, Application, version, Firebase config)
│   ├── composeApp/                  (main app — shared KMP library for Android, iOS, JVM; the desktop app itself)
│   ├── iosApp/                      (Xcode project + Podfile, not a Gradle module)
│   ├── SkyGamesBackend/             (SkyGames Backend — the server: HTTP API, email verification codes, the autonomous system check, see below)
│   ├── SkyGamesBackOffice/          (SkyGames BackOffice — one app for the computer and the phone, KMP JVM + Android: the Blacklist and the switch of the system check, through the server, and the conversation 
│   ├── SkyGamesBackOfficeAndroid/   (the Android application around :SkyGamesBackOffice — application id, manifest, icon, google-services.json; no code)
│   └── XRApp/                       (Quest 3 VR app — Android only, src/main/ only)
├── Libs/
│   ├── A2uiDesktop/                 (Google's A2UI Compose renderer on the desktop — copied from Open Design, see its NOTICE)
│   ├── FlySightApi/                 (BLE device communication — includeBuild, git submodule)
│   └── QuestApi/                    (Quest 3 communication API — Gradle name :QuestApiModule)

# Local configuration (`local.properties`)

> Moved out of `CLAUDE.md` on 2026-08-27, verbatim. Open it on a fresh clone, when a build warns
> about a missing key, or when a sign-in screen names a key you have never heard of.

`local.properties` is not versioned and a fresh clone has none. Copy the versioned template
and fill it in:

```bash
cp local.properties.example local.properties
```

Four keys are expected, and that is the whole list:

| Key | Read by | Needed for | Missing means |
|-----|---------|-----------|---------------|
| `sdk.dir` | the Android Gradle plugin, directly | every Android build | build fails, unless `ANDROID_HOME` is set |
| `google.clientId` | `Apps/composeApp/build.gradle.kts` → `-Dgoogle.clientId` | desktop Google sign-in **only** | build warns; sign-in screen names the missing key |
| `google.clientSecret` | `Apps/composeApp/build.gradle.kts` → `-Dgoogle.clientSecret` | desktop Google sign-in **only** | idem |
| `skyderby.clientId` | `Apps/composeApp/build.gradle.kts` → `BuildConfig.SKYDERBY_CLIENT_ID` | Skyderby sign-in, **Android and iOS** | Skyderby sign-in refuses to start and names the file and the key |

`Libs/FlySightApi` is a separate Gradle build with its own `local.properties`, which needs
`sdk.dir` and nothing else — same `ANDROID_HOME` exception. The CI chain writes it itself
(`.gitlab-ci.yml`), because its runner does not export the variable.

Three things worth knowing before you go looking:

- **Only `skyderby.clientId` affects Android and iOS**, and it affects *only* those two: the
  desktop `SkyderbyServiceDelegate` refuses its one method, the OAuth flow, so Skyderby linking is
  not available on desktop at all and filling this key in changes nothing there. The two Google
  keys are the mirror image — desktop-only —
  Android and iOS sign in through their platform Google SDK, configured by the versioned
  `Apps/composeApp/google-services.json` and `Apps/iosApp/iosApp/GoogleService-Info.plist`.
  This is why the CI chain, which builds only Android and iOS, is indifferent to them.
- **No Firebase key belongs here.** Firebase configuration is versioned, in the two files
  above. On desktop, `firebase::App::Create()` looks for `google-services.json` in the
  *working directory* — which is why `./gradlew :composeApp:run`, running from
  `Apps/composeApp/`, finds it. A `firebase.apiKey` key found in an older `local.properties`
  is a leftover: nothing reads it.
- **The Google OAuth client must be a "Desktop app" client of the same Firebase project** as
  `google-services.json`. The desktop flow exchanges the Google id token against Firebase, so
  a client from another project fails at the second step.

// [SGM-10] Read once and reused by both the jvmArgs below and the warning further down, so
// the value that is shipped and the value that is checked cannot drift apart.
val desktopGoogleClientId = localProperties.getProperty("google.clientId", "")
val desktopGoogleClientSecret = localProperties.getProperty("google.clientSecret", "")

compose.desktop {
    application {
        mainClass = "fr.hozakan.skygames.MainKt"

        // [SGM-41] These two options do not stay on the machine that builds. The Compose
        // Desktop plugin forwards `jvmArgs` to jpackage as `--java-options`, and jpackage
        // writes those into the launcher configuration file of the packaged application — so
        // the Google client secret ships in clear text inside every DMG, MSI and DEB built
        // from a configured clone, readable by anyone who downloads the desktop application.
        // That is accepted, deliberately. An audit already raised it once as a critical
        // finding, and the whole reasoning had to be reconstructed from scratch; this comment
        // is here so that the next audit does not have to do it a third time.
        //
        // Why it is accepted. A person decided it, on SGM-3, after the same secret had been
        // found committed in this repository and taken back out of it: the client secret of an
        // OAuth "Desktop app" client is not a strong secret. An installed application cannot
        // keep one — whatever it ships with, its user can read — and Google nevertheless
        // requires it at the token exchange for that client type, so there is no way of
        // configuring this client that would let us simply drop it.
        //
        // What this published secret does not give away is the authorization code, and that
        // is PKCE's doing — verifiable here rather than taken on trust. In
        // DesktopAuthServiceDelegate (UserModule, jvmMain), `generateCodeVerifier` and
        // `generateCodeChallenge` draw a random verifier and its SHA-256 challenge,
        // `launchGoogleOAuthFlow` puts the challenge on the authorization request, and
        // `exchangeGoogleAuthCode` sends the verifier itself only on the direct call to
        // Google's token endpoint. An intercepted authorization code is therefore useless to
        // whoever holds this secret but not that verifier. Read that as what it says — PKCE
        // protects the code — and not as a verdict on the rest of the flow.
        //
        // Two things this is not. It is not a reason to pass anything else through `jvmArgs`:
        // every value put here is published with the application. And it is not a measurement
        // on a package this project ships — the mechanism above is read off the Compose plugin,
        // and reproduced on a throwaway jpackage image where the option does land in clear text
        // in the launcher `.cfg`, but nobody has yet opened a SkyGames DMG, MSI or DEB and
        // searched it. SGM-30 carries that check.
        jvmArgs(
            "-Dgoogle.clientId=$desktopGoogleClientId",
            "-Dgoogle.clientSecret=$desktopGoogleClientSecret"
        )

        nativeDistributions {
            targetFormats(TargetFormat.Dmg, TargetFormat.Msi, TargetFormat.Deb)
            packageName = "fr.hozakan.

'''

            time.sleep(min(14, max(0.1, end - time.time())))      # the app pings every 14 s

'''

            ok = args.expect_drop

'''

    p.add_argument('--no-ping', action='store_true', help='do not ping while staying connected')
    p.add_argument('--expect-drop', action='store_true', help='the link is expected to end by itself')
    p.add_argument('-v', '--verbose', action='store_true')
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_connect)
'''
assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

**Tool: Bash** — Read how the firmware derives its static random (identity) address

~~~~bash
cd ~/dev/Flysight/flysight-2-firmware && sed -n 950,990p STM32_WPAN/App/app_ble.c; grep -n "a_srd_bd_addr\|BleGetBdAddress\|CFG_STATIC_RANDOM_ADDRESS\|LL_FLASH_GetUDN\|FS_Common_GetRandomBytes\|hw_rng\|HW_RNG_Get" STM32_WPAN/App/app_ble.c Core/Inc/app_conf.h | head -30
~~~~
Result:

~~~~
/**
   * Static random Address
   * The two upper bits shall be set to 1
   * The lowest 32bits is read from the UDN to differentiate between devices
   * The RNG may be used to provide a random number on each power on
   */
#if (CFG_IDENTITY_ADDRESS == GAP_STATIC_RANDOM_ADDR)
#if defined(CFG_STATIC_RANDOM_ADDRESS)
  a_srd_bd_addr[0] = CFG_STATIC_RANDOM_ADDRESS & 0xFFFFFFFF;
  a_srd_bd_addr[1] = (uint32_t)((uint64_t)CFG_STATIC_RANDOM_ADDRESS >> 32);
  a_srd_bd_addr[1] |= 0xC000; /* The two upper bits shall be set to 1 */
#else
  FS_Common_GetRandomBytes(a_srd_bd_addr, 2);
  a_srd_bd_addr[1] |= 0xC000; /* The two upper bits shall be set to 1 */
#endif /* CFG_STATIC_RANDOM_ADDRESS */
#endif

#if (CFG_BLE_ADDRESS_TYPE == GAP_STATIC_RANDOM_ADDR)
#endif

#if (CFG_BLE_ADDRESS_TYPE != PUBLIC_ADDR)
  ret = aci_hal_write_config_data(CONFIG_DATA_RANDOM_ADDRESS_OFFSET, CONFIG_DATA_RANDOM_ADDRESS_LEN, (uint8_t*)a_srd_bd_addr);
  if (ret != BLE_STATUS_SUCCESS)
  {
    APP_DBG_MSG("  Fail   : aci_hal_write_config_data command - CONFIG_DATA_RANDOM_ADDRESS_OFFSET, result: 0x%x \n", ret);
  }
  else
  {
    APP_DBG_MSG("  Success: aci_hal_write_config_data command - CONFIG_DATA_RANDOM_ADDRESS_OFFSET\n");
    APP_DBG_MSG("  Random Bluetooth Address: %02x:%02x:%02x:%02x:%02x:%02x\n", (uint8_t)(a_srd_bd_addr[1] >> 8),
                                                                               (uint8_t)(a_srd_bd_addr[1]),
                                                                               (uint8_t)(a_srd_bd_addr[0] >> 24),
                                                                               (uint8_t)(a_srd_bd_addr[0] >> 16),
                                                                               (uint8_t)(a_srd_bd_addr[0] >> 8),
                                                                               (uint8_t)(a_srd_bd_addr[0]));
  }
#endif /* CFG_BLE_ADDRESS_TYPE != GAP_PUBLIC_ADDR */
