**Tool: Bash** — Make the cable script compare the state file field by field and flag a reading taken with the cable back in

~~~~bash
cd /home/[user]/dev/Flysight/flysight-2-firmware/debug_ble/linux; python3 - <<'PY'
p='state_real_unplug.py'; s=open(p).read()
def swap(old,new):
    global s
    assert s.count(old)==1,(s.count(old),old[:60]); s=s.replace(old,new)
swap("PATIENCE = 600      # seconds given to the person who holds the cable",
     "PATIENCE = 1800     # seconds given to the person who holds the cable")
swap("""    result = {'bytes': len(data), 'keys': keys, 'temp': fields.get('Temp_Folder', '?'), 'active': fields.get('Active_Mode', '?'),
              'tmp': os.path.exists(os.path.join(mount, 'FLYSIGHT.TMP')), 'digest': hashlib.sha1(data).hexdigest()[:8]}""",
"""    result = {'bytes': len(data), 'keys': keys, 'temp': fields.get('Temp_Folder', '?'), 'active': fields.get('Active_Mode', '?'),
              'tmp': os.path.exists(os.path.join(mount, 'FLYSIGHT.TMP')), 'digest': hashlib.sha1(data).hexdigest()[:8], 'fields': fields}""")
swap("""    s = build.snap()
    log('%s | PULL 1, card mounted on the PC, firmware left alone: %d s later %s, %s' % (build.name, SETTLE, s, keys_word(reference, s.keys)))
    return before, reference
""","""    back = present(FLYSIGHT)
    s = build.snap()
    log('%s | PULL 1, card mounted on the PC, firmware left alone: %d s later %s, %s%s' % (build.name, SETTLE, s, keys_word(reference, s.keys),
        ' | NOT A VALID READING: the cable was back in before it' if back else ''))
    return before, reference
""")
swap("""    same = all(before.get(k) == after.get(k) for k in ('digest', 'keys', 'temp', 'tmp')) and 'digest' in after
    log('%s | plugged back in: the PC reads %s -> %s' % (build.name, after['text'], 'THE SAME FILE as before the pull' if same else 'NOT the same as before the pull'))
""","""    if 'fields' not in before or 'fields' not in after:
        log('%s | plugged back in: the PC reads %s -> NOTHING TO COMPARE' % (build.name, after['text']))
        return
    a, b = before['fields'], after['fields']
    changed = sorted(k for k in set(a) | set(b) if a.get(k) != b.get(k))
    # the two versions of the radio firmware read 8.0.0 until the second processor has started,
    # so a file written at start-up and a file written later differ there; their values are no secret
    versions = ['%s %s -> %s' % (k, a.get(k), b.get(k)) for k in changed if k in ('FUS_Ver', 'Stack_Ver')]
    others = [k for k in changed if k not in ('FUS_Ver', 'Stack_Ver')]
    verdict = 'THE SAME FILE as before the pull' if not changed else \\
              'the same as before the pull but for %s' % ', '.join(versions) if not others else \\
              'NOT THE SAME as before the pull: %s differ' % ', '.join(others + versions)
    log('%s | plugged back in: the PC reads %s -> %s%s' % (build.name, after['text'], verdict,
        '' if before['tmp'] == after['tmp'] else ' | FLYSIGHT.TMP appeared or went'))
""")
open(p,'w').write(s)
PY
python3 -m py_compile state_real_unplug.py && echo ok
~~~~

## Assistant (02:12)

Le test du câble s'est arrêté au sixième build : le script a attendu dix minutes un débranchement qui n'est pas venu. Les cinq premiers builds sont complets, il reste `branch-statefix`.

**Ne touche plus au câble pour l'instant.** J'ai lancé à la place le test du mode config avec un dossier `/config`, qui est entièrement automatique et dure environ 20 minutes sur les six builds. Dès qu'il est fini, je te redemande quatre débranchements pour terminer le dernier build.

## Câble réellement arraché, cinq builds sur six

| Build | Débranchement, carte montée | Débranchement après éjection | Reset pendant l'écriture |
|---|---|---|---|
| `master` sans correctif | clés gardées | 1 écriture, 20 ms | non testé |
| `master` avec correctif | clés gardées | 1 écriture, 36 ms | non testé |
| `develop` sans correctif | clés gardées | 1 écriture, 19 ms | non testé |
| `develop` avec correctif | clés gardées | 1 écriture, 35 ms | non testé |
| branche sans correctif | clés gardées | 1 écriture, 20 ms | **clés changées**, `Temp_Folder` remis à 0000 |
| branche avec correctif | à faire | à faire | à faire |

- **Pas de rebond :** un vrai débranchement ne déclenche qu'une seule écriture du fichier d'état, sur les cinq builds mesurés.
- **Fichier relu depuis le PC :** après chaque rebranchement, mêmes clés, même `Temp_Folder`, pas de `FLYSIGHT.TMP`.
- **L'octet de différence :** écrit au démarrage, le fichier donne `8.0.0` pour les deux versions de la pile radio. Je pense que c'est parce que le second processeur n'a pas encore démarré, et que la valeur écrite plus tard est plus longue d'un caractère ; je le confirme au dernier build.
- **Sans le correctif, le reset fait perdre tout le fichier**, pas seulement les clés : `Temp_Folder` repart de 0000 et les prochaines sessions réécriront donc `TEMP/0001` et suivants.

Le premier résultat du mode config est bon : `master` sans correctif parcourt les trois fichiers de `/config` et revient en veille avec les clés gardées.

    ws = words_of(str(i))
    raw = struct.pack('<%dI' % len(ws), *ws)[shift:]
    if size is not None:
        raw = raw[:size]
    if label == 'fs':
        say('fs: fs_type=%d drv=%d n_fats=%d   first 16 bytes: %s' % (raw[0], raw[1], raw[2], raw[:16].hex()))
        # the sector window is the last 512 bytes of the structure (_MAX_SS == 512)
        win = raw[len(raw) - 512:len(raw)] if len(raw) >= 512 else b''

        base = addr
    stack += ws
say('return addresses left on the stack below and above SP (deepest first):')
seen = 0
for n, w in enumerate(stack):
    if 0x08000000 <= w < 0x08100000 and (w & 1):
        name = where(w - 1)
        if not name.startswith('??'):
            say('  [SP%+5d] 0x%08x %s' % (base + 4 * n - int(regs.get('SP', '0'), 16), w, name))
            seen += 1
say('%d code addresses found' % seen)
~~~~

#!/bin/bash
# Tries to get again the stop in Error_Handler seen once when active mode started after config
# mode, with a /config folder, on the branch without the state-file fix. Reads the stopped
# firmware if it happens.   usage: repro_stop.sh [variant] [tries]
S="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
LNX=~/dev/Flysight/flysight-2-firmware/debug_ble/linux
V="${1:-branch-nostatefix}"; TRIES="${2:-14}"
E=$S/four/$V/build/$V.elf
card() { for d in /media/$USER/*/; do [ -f "$d/CONFIG.TXT" ] && { echo "${d%/}"; return 0; }; done; return 1; }
mounted() { for i in $(seq 1 60); do card > /dev/null && return 0; sleep 1; done; return 1; }
ocd() { printf 'stm32wbx.cpu configure -event examine-end {}\ninit\nproc rd8 {a} { return [lindex [read_memory $a 8 1] 0] }\n%s\nexit\n' "$1" > "$S/modes/repro.tcl"; timeout 60 openocd -f interface/stlink.cfg -c "transport select hla_swd" -f target/stm32wbx.cfg -f "$S/modes/repro.tcl" 2>&1; }
flash() { timeout 120 openocd -f interface/stlink.cfg -c "transport select hla_swd" -f target/stm32wbx.cfg -c "program $1 verify reset exit" 2>&1 | grep -E "Verified|Error"; sleep 4; }
leave_usb() {
  sync
  M="$(card)" && udisksctl unmount -b "$(findmnt -no SOURCE "$M")" 2>&1 | head -1
  ocd 'mww 0x48000018 0x40000
mwb 0x48000000 [expr {([rd8 0x48000000] & ~0x30) | 0x10}]
sleep 3000' | grep -i "error" | head -2
}
vbus_free() { ocd 'mwb 0x48000000 [expr {[rd8 0x48000000] & ~0x30}]' | grep -i "error" | head -2; }

echo "################ the folder   $(date +%H:%M:%S)"
mounted || { echo "CARD NOT MOUNTED: nothing done"; exit 1; }
M="$(card)"
if [ ! -d "$M/CONFIG" ]; then
  mkdir "$M/CONFIG"
  for N in ALPHA BRAVO CHARLIE; do
    printf '; %s: a test configuration for config mode\r\n\r\nInit_File: %s ; Announces this configuration\r\n' "$N" "$(echo $N | tr A-Z a-z)" > "$M/CONFIG/$N.TXT"
  done
fi
sync
leave_usb
echo "################ $V   $(date +%H:%M:%S)"
flash $E
python3 $LNX/state_modes.py $E unplugged-start 2>&1 | grep -v "the fix$"
python3 $LNX/state_modes.py $E config-through 1 2>&1 | grep -v "the fix$" | cut -c1-400
STOPPED=0
for I in $(seq 1 $TRIES); do
  OUT="$(python3 $LNX/state_modes.py $E config-select 1 2>&1 | grep -v "the fix$")"
  echo "try $I  $(date +%H:%M:%S)  $(echo "$OUT" | cut -c1-620)"
  if echo "$OUT" | grep -q "Error_Handler"; then
    STOPPED=1
    echo "################ STOPPED: what the firmware holds   $(date +%H:%M:%S)"
    python3 $LNX/postmortem.py $E "$S/modes/repro_postmortem.txt" 2>&1 | cut -c1-400
    break
  fi
done
echo "REPRO_RESULT stopped=$STOPPED after $I tries"
echo "REPRO_DONE $(date +%H:%M:%S)"
~~~~

#!/bin/bash
# After the tests of config mode: takes the three test files and their folder off the card,
# puts the bench build back and empties Config_File.
S="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
LNX=~/dev/Flysight/flysight-2-firmware/debug_ble/linux
E=$S/four/branch-statefix/build/branch-statefix.elf
card() { for d in /media/$USER/*/; do [ -f "$d/CONFIG.TXT" ] && { echo "${d%/}"; return 0; }; done; return 1; }
mounted() { for i in $(seq 1 60); do card > /dev/null && return 0; sleep 1; done; return 1; }
ocd() { printf 'stm32wbx.cpu configure -event examine-end {}\ninit\nproc rd8 {a} { return [lindex [read_memory $a 8 1] 0] }\n%s\nexit\n' "$1" > "$S/modes/cleanup.tcl"; timeout 60 openocd -f interface/stlink.cfg -c "transport select hla_swd" -f target/stm32wbx.cfg -f "$S/modes/cleanup.tcl" 2>&1; }
mounted || { echo "CARD NOT MOUNTED: nothing done"; exit 1; }
M="$(card)"
if [ -d "$M/CONFIG" ]; then
  rm -f "$M/CONFIG/ALPHA.TXT" "$M/CONFIG/BRAVO.TXT" "$M/CONFIG/CHARLIE.TXT" && rmdir "$M/CONFIG"
fi
sync
echo "/config on the card: $([ -e "$M/CONFIG" ] && echo STILL THERE || echo removed)"
udisksctl unmount -b "$(findmnt -no SOURCE "$M")" 2>&1 | head -1
ocd 'mww 0x48000018 0x40000
mwb 0x48000000 [expr {([rd8 0x48000000] & ~0x30) | 0x10}]
sleep 3000' | grep -i "error" | head -2
timeout 120 openocd -f interface/stlink.cfg -c "transport select hla_swd" -f target/stm32wbx.cfg -c "program $E verify reset exit" 2>&1 | grep -E "Verified|Error"
sleep 4
python3 $LNX/state_modes.py $E unplugged-start 2>&1 | grep -v "the fix$"
python3 $LNX/state_modes.py $E config 1 2>&1 | grep -v "the fix$" | cut -c1-700
mounted && { M="$(card)"; echo "Config_File line on the card: $(grep -a "^Config_File" "$M/FLYSIGHT.TXT" | tr -d '\r')|"; echo "root of the card: $(ls -A "$M" | tr '\n' '|')"; }
echo CLEANUP_DONE $(date +%H:%M:%S)
~~~~

			logState = LOG_STATE_FAILED;
			return HAL_ERROR;

		if (!FS_Log_AcquireSensorBatchBuffer())
		{
			f_close(&sensorFile);
			logState = LOG_STATE_FAILED;
			return HAL_ERROR;
		}
		FS_Log_WriteSensorHeader();

	if (enable_flags & FS_LOG_ENABLE_EVENT)

## Assistant (02:46)

Les deux tests sont faits sur les six builds et le correctif les passe tous. Un arrêt dans `Error_Handler`, vu une seule fois sur la branche sans le correctif, reste inexpliqué. Rien n'est commité ni poussé.

## Câble réellement arraché

| Build | Arraché, carte montée | Arraché après éjection | Arraché + reset pendant l'écriture |
|---|---|---|---|
| `master` | OK | 1 écriture, 20 ms | non lancé |
| `master` + correctif | OK | 1 écriture, 36 ms | non lancé |
| `develop` | OK | 1 écriture, 19 ms | non lancé |
| `develop` + correctif | OK | 1 écriture, 35 ms | non lancé |
| branche sans correctif | OK | 1 écriture, 20 ms | **clés changées** |
| branche avec correctif | OK | 1 écriture, 27 ms | clés gardées |

- **« OK »** : quatre secondes après l'arrachage le firmware dort avec les mêmes clés. Une fois rebranché, le PC relit un `FLYSIGHT.TXT` complet, mêmes clés, même `Temp_Folder`, sans `FLYSIGHT.TMP`.
- **Pas de rebond** : une seule écriture du fichier d'état par arrachage.
- **L'octet de différence** : `FUS_Ver` et `Stack_Ver` valent `8.0.0` dans un fichier écrit au démarrage, puis `1.2.0` et `1.19.0`. Je l'ai lu champ par champ sur le dernier build ; c'est pareil avec et sans le correctif.
- **Sans le correctif, le reset fait perdre tout le fichier** : `Temp_Folder` repart de 0000 et les sessions suivantes écrasent `TEMP/0001` et les suivantes.

## Mode config avec un dossier `/config`

La carte a reçu trois fichiers (`ALPHA.TXT`, `BRAVO.TXT`, `CHARLIE.TXT`). Ils sont retirés depuis.

| Test | Sans le correctif | Avec le correctif |
|---|---|---|
| Parcours des trois fichiers sans appui | OK sur les trois | OK sur les trois |
| Appui pendant l'annonce, puis mode actif | OK 2/2 sur `master` et `develop` ; **un arrêt** puis OK 14/14 sur la branche | OK 2/2 sur les trois |
| Reset pendant l'écriture en quittant le mode config | clés changées, `Config_File` vidé | clés et `Config_File` gardés, 2/2 sur les trois |

- **Fichier retenu** : `ALPHA.TXT`, le premier, alors que je visais le deuxième. Le nom est identique dans le firmware et dans le fichier relu par le PC.
- **Écriture depuis `/config`** : le mode actif écrit l'état alors que `/config` est le répertoire courant, et aucun fichier d'état n'y apparaît.
- **Pas testé** : le mode config avec des fichiers audio à jouer, la carte n'ayant pas de dossier `/audio`.

## L'arrêt inexpliqué

- **Où** : branche sans le correctif, première entrée en mode actif après le mode config.
- **Ce que je sais** : l'arrêt est dans `FS_ActiveMode_Init()`, après l'ouverture des fichiers de session, donc dans l'audio, l'ADC, le GNSS ou les capteurs.
- **Ce que j'ai perdu** : l'état du firmware arrêté. La chaîne de tests a continué et flashé le build suivant avant que je le lise.
- **Reproduction** : 14 nouveaux essais sur le même build, aucun arrêt.
- **Pas le blocage microSD connu, a priori** : ce build contient les 50 ms, et la carte venait d'être montée et écrite.

## État du banc

- **Firmware** : la branche avec les trois correctifs, câble branché, carte montée.
- **Clés BLE** : elles ont encore changé. Mac, Android, iPad et ce PC doivent refaire l'appairage.
- **`FILL.BIN`** : toujours dans la corbeille de la carte. Ne la vide pas ; `chkdsk /f` sous Windows ou un formatage règle le problème.

## Ce qui attend ta décision

Le rapport et les deux README contiennent les nouveaux tableaux, et un nouveau script pilote le test du câble. Tout cela est non commité, et `9762e0e` est toujours local. Dis-moi si tu veux le commit, et s'il faut pousser.

Give up the second flysight.txt at the first write that fails

On a card with no free cluster FatFs searches the whole FAT before each write
fails, and the state was written to flysight.tmp one f_printf() at a time:
136 searches. On a 2 GB card filled for real, FS_State_Write() took 43 s, at
every start, every time active mode started and after every USB unplug. It
takes 20 ms there without the previous commit.

Stop at the first f_printf() that does not go through, and write in place as
before. FS_State_Write() then takes 0.34 s on that card: one search, then the
write.

Measured with a test build that gives one file every free cluster of the card
(the PC then reports 0 KB free), on master, on develop and on this branch.
The earlier test of a full card had the debugger refuse the clusters, which

debug_ble: test the state-file fix outside start-up and on the bench by hand

Section 7 of the report said the fix had been exercised at start-up only. It
now holds the tests that were missing, on the same six builds each time: this
branch, master and develop, without the fix and with it.

- Active mode, start mode and config mode entered and left, USB unplugged with
  a PC as host, resets just after the file to write is opened, the time the
  write takes, and a card filled for real (state_modes.py,
  state_write_time.sh, card-fill-test.patch). The full card is what showed
  the 43 s of the first commit of the fix.
- A cable really pulled out, 15 times by hand (state_real_unplug.py, which
  says when to pull and sees that it was done). One write of the state file
  per pull, 19 to 20 ms without the fix and 27 to 36 ms with it; keys kept.
  With a reset during that write the keys change without the fix and the
  whole file is lost, Temp_Folder included; they are kept with it.
- Config mode with a /config folder of three files: the name chosen is the
  one written and read back, active mode then writes the state from inside
  /config without leaving a file there, and a reset as the press leaves
  config mode changes the keys without the fix only.

Two things are written down as not explained or not repaired:

- once, on the branch without the fix, active mode stopped in Error_Handler
  after config mode. The firmware was not read before the next flash, and 14
  more runs did not stop;
- the bench card keeps a directory entry for the FILL.BIN of the full-card
  test. The PC deleted it, the last sector of that deletion was still in the
  RAM cache of USB mode when the next flash reset the FlySight. The READMEs
  say how to remove it, and that the cable has to come out before a flash.

729:<h3 class="step">Why I am not sure</h3>
----
<h3 class="step">Why I am not sure</h3>
<p><code>FS_State_Write()</code> does not only run at start-up. <code>FS_ActiveMode_Init()</code> and <code>FS_StartMode_Init()</code> call <code>FS_State_NextSession()</code>, which increments <code>Temp_Folder</code>, draws a new <code>Session_ID</code> and writes the file. It also runs when config mode ends (<code>FS_State_SetConfigFilename()</code>) and after USB is unplugged (<code>FS_State_Update()</code>).</p>
<p>So with this fix, entering active mode no longer rewrites <code>flysight.txt</code> in place: it writes a second file, removes the first and renames the second. What that changes, from the tests above:</p>
<ul>
  <li>the write takes 10 to 20 ms longer, 31 to 43 ms where it took 20 to 24, before the files of the session are opened; one measurement out of eighteen took 93 ms;</li>
  <li>on a card with no free cluster it takes about a third of a second instead of 20 ms: one search of the FAT, then the write in place. That time grows with the size of the FAT, and this card has a small one;</li>
  <li>a <code>FLYSIGHT.TMP</code> stays on the card after a write that did not finish, until the next write by a firmware that has the fix.</li>
</ul>
<div class="callout warn">
<p><strong>Still not tested.</strong> A jump, or any active mode longer than a few seconds on a bench. A reset that does not come from the debugger. Config mode with audio files to play. Another card: this one holds a 2 GB FAT16 volume with 32 KB clusters. A <code>flysight.txt</code> already emptied by a firmware without the fix stays lost.</p>
</div>
<p><strong>What the tests left on the bench.</strong> The keys of the FlySight changed many times: every device bonded with it has to forget it and pair again. Sessions were added to <code>TEMP</code> on its card, about 3.7 MB. And the card still lists the <code>FILL.BIN</code> of the full-card test although its space is free: the PC deleted it, the firmware kept the last sector of that deletion in the RAM cache of its USB mode, and the flash that followed reset it before the sector reached the card. Linux never asks the FlySight to write that cache (<q>Assuming drive cache: write through</q>); it is written when USB mode ends. The entry, since moved to the trash folder of the card, has to be removed with <code>chkdsk /f</code> or <code>fsck.vfat</code>, or by formatting the card, not from a file manager and not by emptying that trash; the details are in <code>linux/README.md</code>.</p>

<p>Found while testing from Linux, then reproduced on purpose. It is two commits on the branch, <em>Keep the previous flysight.txt until the new one is written</em> (<code>cb3d5f0</code>) and <em>Give up the second flysight.txt at the first write that fails</em> (<code>9762e0e</code>). They are not in the patch of <a href="#patch">section 6</a>: the three fixes above do not need them.</p>

<h3 class="step">Glossary</h3>
<dl>
  <dt>State file</dt>
  <dd><code>/flysight.txt</code> on the microSD card. Besides the settings a user may edit, it holds what the firmware must find again at the next start: <code>BLE_IRK</code> and <code>BLE_ERK</code> (see <a href="#b3">bug 3</a>), <code>Session_ID</code>, <code>Temp_Folder</code>, <code>Config_File</code>.</dd>
  <dt><code>FA_CREATE_ALWAYS</code></dt>
  <dd>The FatFs option that opens a file for writing and, if it exists, empties it first.</dd>
</dl>

<h3 class="step">Problem</h3>
<p><code>FS_State_Init()</code> runs at every start. It reads the state file, then writes it back from memory:</p>
<div class="file">FlySight/state.c</div>
<pre><code>void FS_State_Init(void)
{
	FS_ResourceManager_RequestResource(FS_RESOURCE_FATFS);
	FS_State_Read();
	FS_State_Write();                              <span class="cm">// at every start</span>
	FS_ResourceManager_ReleaseResource(FS_RESOURCE_FATFS);
}

static void FS_State_Write(void)
{
	...
	if (f_open(&amp;stateFile, "/flysight.txt", FA_WRITE|FA_CREATE_ALWAYS) != FR_OK)   <span class="cm">// the file is empty from here...</span>
	...
	f_close(&amp;stateFile);                                                          <span class="cm">// ...to here</span>
}</code></pre>
<p>Between those two lines the card holds an empty <code>flysight.txt</code>, and a reset there leaves it empty. At the next start the firmware opens it, reads no <code>BLE_IRK</code> and no <code>BLE_ERK</code>, draws new ones and writes them. The change is permanent: bonded devices no longer recognise the FlySight and have to pair again, and the other values of the file are back to their defaults.</p>
<p><strong>Measured</strong> on the bench build of the branch, with breakpoints on three starts: the write begins 125 ms after the reset, the file is emptied at 130 ms and closed at 145 ms. A reset sent over SWD with the firmware stopped in <code>FS_State_Write()</code> changed the keys 6 times out of 6. Each time the next start was caught at the call that draws the new IRK, and the root directory it had just read showed <code>FLYSIGHT.TXT</code> with a size of 0 and no cluster. Resets sent 50 ms earlier (4), after the file is closed (68) or with the card off (17) all kept the keys. The keys were compared by the SHA-1 of what the firmware holds in memory.</p>
<p>The reset always came from the debugger. No real-life cause was tried, such as a battery too low to get through a start.</p>

<h3 class="step">Proposed fix</h3>
<p>Write the new state next to the previous one, and replace the previous one only once the new one is complete. A reset between the removal and the renaming leaves only the new file, which the next start puts in place. When the new file cannot be written, give it up at the first write that fails and write in place as before:</p>
<div class="file">FlySight/state.c</div>
<pre><code><span class="add">+#define STATE_FILE "/flysight.txt"
+#define STATE_TEMP "/flysight.tmp"</span>
 ...
 void FS_State_Read(void)
 {
 	...
......
+	if (f_open(&amp;stateFile, STATE_FILE, FA_WRITE|FA_CREATE_ALWAYS) != FR_OK)
+	{
+		Error_Handler();
+	}
+	FS_State_WriteContent();</span>
 }</code></pre>
<p>The last branch of <code>FS_State_Write()</code> is there for a card with no free cluster. The code before the fix gets through on such a card, because emptying the file frees the cluster it writes to next; with that branch a full card behaves as it did before the fix, window included.</p>
<p>The two checks in <code>FS_State_WriteContent()</code> both come from the way FatFs treats a write that
[... output cut at 4000 characters, 5003 in total ...]

Rules the user gave on 2026-10-09 for `debug_ble/ble-pairing-fixes-report.html`, the report that is sent to the firmware's maintainer:

- Every section on a defect follows **glossary > problem > proposed fix** (then tests), and nothing else as a heading. A word used in the section is defined in its glossary first. ("you need to respect the vocabulary>issue>solution principle"; asked a first time for sections 8 and 9.)
- **No statement of doubt.** No "I am not sure", no "why I am not sure" block, even one the user asked for earlier. ("we are sending a report, we need to be sure".) What was a doubt becomes either a measured part of the problem, a measured cost of the fix, or an item of a "Limits of the tests" card in the same form as the other sections.
- **No state of the workbench.** Keys that changed on the bench FlySight, files left on its card, what has to be re-paired: none of it. ("on se fou, dans un rapport, de l'etat du workbench".)
- **No side observation that is not explained** and does not bear on the fix (the user had the paragraph on an unexplained stop removed: "On s'en fou enleve").

**Why:** the report is read by someone outside who has to decide on the fixes; it must state what is established.

**How to apply:** bench housekeeping, hand-over notes and unexplained observations go to `debug_ble/README.md` and `debug_ble/linux/README.md`, not the report. My interpretation: test limits stay allowed, since the user kept and reorganised the "Limits" cards; a result stays exact when its explanation is removed (a count, not a rounded "OK").

128	<p><strong>Why start a new pairing process.</strong> To trigger advertising when the FlySight does not restart it. A bug was found about that (<a href="#b2">bug 2</a>). During development it also makes the work a lot faster.</p>
129	
130	<h2 id="found">What the investigation found</h2>
131	<ul>
132	  <li><strong>The bug is confirmed.</strong> After these three steps the Mac cannot connect to the FlySight, exactly as reported. It was reproduced on unmodified <code>master</code> and <code>develop</code>, and with the fix the Mac connects (<a href="#b1">bug 1</a>).</li>
133	  <li><strong>Its cause is not the suspected one.</strong> The Mac does recognise the FlySight: once bonded, it shows it under one and the same identifier when the FlySight is idle, when it is back in pairing mode, and after it reboots. What fails is the connection request itself, which the FlySight's radio controller discards before the firmware hears of it.</li>
134	  <li><strong>Android and iOS are not affected.</strong> An Android phone and an iPad were tested: both go through the same sequence on unmodified firmware. They connect in a different way from the Mac, which the controller accepts. The difference between the platforms is in the address the <em>host</em> connects from, not in how it identifies the FlySight.</li>
135	  <li><strong>Linux is not affected by bug 1 either.</strong> A Linux PC connects from its identity address, as the Mac does, and still connects on all four builds, patched or not (<a href="#table-c">table C</a>). What stopped it was on the host: BlueZ refuses the pairing unless the application has registered a pairing agent.</li>
136	  <li><strong>A FlySight that stops advertising</strong> was reproduced on <code>develop</code>: a pairing window that expires unused ends with no advertising at all (<a href="#b2">bug 2</a>). This one concerns every platform. On <code>develop</code> the two chain for a Mac: the bonded Mac cannot connect during the window, the window expires unused, and the FlySight goes silent.</li>
137	  <li>A third, unrelated defect was found on the way (<a href="#b3">bug 3</a>).</li>
138	</ul>
139	<p><strong>An app-side issue, not a firmware one.</strong> For a host that is <em>not</em> bonded, the identifier does change. The FlySight advertises from a private address that changes each time advertising restarts, and only a bonded host can follow it. Before it was paired, the iPad listed the same FlySight under four different identifiers over four advertising runs. An entry obtained before pairing mode started is therefore dead once pairing mode starts: an app that still offers it, or that has saved it, waits forever on an identifier that no longer exists. This is how BLE privacy is meant to behave, so the handling belongs in the app: its scan list must only hold what is advertising now, and it should not keep a FlySight it has never connected to.</p>

676	<p>The last branch of <code>FS_State_Write()</code> is there for a card with no free cluster. The code before the fix gets through on such a card, because emptying the file frees the cluster it writes to next; with that branch a full card behaves as it did before the fix, window included.</p>
677	<p>The two checks in <code>FS_State_WriteContent()</code> both come from the way FatFs treats a write that finds no room: it does not report it as an error, and it searches the whole FAT before each one fails. Without the check of the last write, a good file would have been replaced by an incomplete one. With that check alone, which is the first of the two commits, writing the state took 43 s on a card that was really full, one search for each of 136 writes: the check of the first write is the second commit.</p>

Result:

~~~~
=========== 89d5e1c
Fix HardFault at boot when USB is plugged in

While start-up waits for CPU2, the sequencer runs every pending task. With
VBUS present at boot, FS_Mode_Update is pending and calls Custom_Mode_Update,
which queued a BLE packet and set the BLE TX queue task before
BLE_TX_Queue_Init() had registered it. The sequencer then called a NULL
callback (HardFault, INVSTATE).

Only schedule the transmit task once it is registered, keep packets queued
before that, and send them from BLE_TX_Queue_Init() so the Mode
characteristic still reflects the current mode.

 1 file changed, 25 insertions(+), 5 deletions(-)
=========== aac9740
Run FS_Mode_Update with the HCI command tasks

BLE_StatusNot pauses every task listed in CFG_Task_Id_With_HCI_Cmd_t while an
HCI command is pending, so that no second command is sent. FS_Mode_Update can
send commands (FS_State_Update -> APP_BLE_UpdateDeviceName on USB removal,
pairing mode) but was in the no-HCI list, so it could run during another
task's HCI wait and block both commands.

Measured with 40-cycle USB unplug/plug runs: 1 block in ~130 cycles before,
0 in 400 after.

 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
=========== 984f4b2
Remove unused CubeMX stubs and silence unused-variable warnings

custom_app.c still carried 16 generated Update_Char/Send_* functions that
nothing calls (master removed them). activelook_client.c has three variables
that are only read by APP_DBG_MSG, which is empty without traces.

The build now has the same three warnings as master.

 2 files changed, 3 insertions(+), 339 deletions(-)
=========== dab59f0
Stop USB before flushing the storage cache on VBUS loss

FS_USBMode_DeInit flushed the USB mass-storage write cache while the USB
device was still attached. A host command arriving during the flush made the
USB interrupt use the microSD while the flush was using it from the task, and
the SPI/DMA transfer in SPIx_WriteReadData (which waits with no timeout) could
then never complete, leaving the firmware stuck or in Error_Handler.

Call USBD_LL_Stop() first. USBD_DeInit() already starts with it, so this only
moves the disconnection before the flush.

Reproduced with a host writing to the card while VBUS is faked low over
ST-Link: 4 of 12 unplugs stalled on this branch and 1 of 12 on master. With
this change 0 of 24 stalled, and 256 KB written just before the unplug is
intact after replugging.

 1 file changed, 7 insertions(+)
=========== first-session notes on the base of the branch
~~~~

Why bug 1 does not apply here: with `Privacy` off, a Linux host gives the FlySight no identity
resolving key when it bonds, and the controller only ignores a peer's identity address when it
holds such a key for it. That last part is the specification as I read it, not something
measured; what is measured is that the connection goes through with the fix off.

So on Linux the firmware was never the obstacle. Without an agent, BlueZ keeps the adapter

Links: [{"title":"Privacy and Tracking#","url":"https://docs.silabs.com/btmesh/9.1.0/bluetooth-application-security-design-considerations/03-privacy-and-tracking"},{"title":"Privacy and Tracking#","url":"https://docs.silabs.com/btmesh/9.0.2/bluetooth-application-security-design-considerations/03-privacy-and-tracking"},{"title":"Address Resolving List#","url":"https://docs.silabs.com/d/bluetooth-stack-api/6.2.0/sl-bt-resolving-list"},{"title":"Address Resolving List#","url":"https://docs.silabs.com/bluetooth/7.1.1/bluetooth-stack-api/sl-bt-resolving-list"},{"title":"Address Resolving List#","url":"https://docs.silabs.com/bluetooth/11.1.0/bluetooth-stack-api/sl-bt-resolving-list"},{"title":"Address Resolving List#","url":"https://docs.silabs.com/bluetooth/7.3.0/bluetooth-stack-api/sl-bt-resolving-list"},{"title":"Address Resolving List#","url":"https://docs.silabs.com/bluetooth/6.0.0/bluetooth-stack-api/sl-bt-resolving-list"},{"title":"Address Resolving List#","url":"https://docs.silabs.com/bluetooth/6.1.0/bluetooth-stack-api/sl-bt-resolving-list"},{"title":"Address Resolving List#","url":"https://docs.silabs.com/bluetooth/9.1.0/bluetooth-stack-api/sl-bt-resolving-list"},{"title":"bt 2020 privacy protection mechanisms in bluetooth technology","url":"https://www.ellisys.com/seminars/bt_2020_privacy_protection_mechanisms_in_bluetooth_technology.pdf"}]

The search didn't return the Bluetooth Core Specification text. The results are Silicon Labs stack documentation and an Ellisys seminar deck, so the points below are secondhand and should be checked against the spec.

**Network privacy mode:** The Silicon Labs security guide treats this as a receive-side restriction. Identity-address advertisements from peers that have distributed their IRK are refused, and only resolvable private addresses are valid for those peers. The same guide adds that a remote device without the Resolvable Private Address Only characteristic may still use its Identity Address over the air.

**Controller behavior:** Silicon Labs' API reference describes the controller side. Under the network setting, the controller accepts Resolvable Private Addresses only from the peer device. Packets that carry the peer's identity address get rejected when that peer's non-zero IRK is in the resolving list, which the reference describes as the stricter default that enforces privacy on the peer ().

**Device privacy mode:** This setting is more permissive. The controller accepts both RPAs and identity addresses, which lets a peer keep using its identity address even after distributing its IRK. Because of that, the local controller does not enforce the peer's network privacy ().

**The all-zero IRK case:** None of the results address an all-zero peer IRK. The Silicon Labs wording ties the rejection rule to a non-zero IRK, which suggests an all-zero entry falls outside it. That is an inference from wording, though, and the sources don't say how a controller handles that entry.

**Next steps:** To confirm the "shall not accept" language and the all-zero IRK behavior, pull the Core Specification from the Bluetooth SIG specifications page and search its privacy and resolving-list sections. I can run one more targeted search for the spec text if you want.

On Linux, reading a secure characteristic does not start the pairing. BlueZ
refuses the "Just Works" pairing of a FlySight, triggered by that read or
requested with Device1.Pair, unless the application has registered a pairing
agent.

     *   **Initiation:** After connecting to a FlySight 2 in Pairing Request Mode, the central device *must* initiate bonding to establish a secure, encrypted link and be added to the whitelist.
     *   **Security:** FlySight 2 requests **Security Mode 1, Level 2** (Authenticated pairing with encryption, No MITM protection). It uses the **Just Works** association model (as it has NoInput/NoOutput capabilities).
     *   **Triggering Pairing:** Since the peripheral (FlySight) cannot force pairing, the central device must trigger it. A reliable method is to attempt to **read a secure characteristic** (e.g., `FT_Packet_In` UUID `0
+    *   **Linux (BlueZ):** Reading a secure characteristic is not enough there. BlueZ refuses the "Just Works" pairing, whether triggered by that read or requested with `Device1.Pair`, unless the application has registe
     *   **Completion:** Once pairing is complete, the central device should store the bonding information (keys) provided by the BLE stack for future use. The FlySight stores the central's identity.

+    *   **Linux (BlueZ):** Reading a secure characteristic is not enough there. BlueZ refuses the "Just Works" pairing, whether triggered by that read or requested with `Device1.Pair`, unless the application has registered a pairing agent (`org.bluez.AgentManager1.RegisterAgent`); without one the adapter is not even bondable. With an agent registered, call `Device1.Pair` after connecting. Measured with BlueZ 5.72: without an agent the FlySight reports a failed pairing (reason `0x0c`) and closes the link at the 30-second timeout.

Linux: the same tests from a Linux PC, and three more bugs
Added on 9 October 2026, after the report above. Same board, same commits of master (9ec7186) and develop (e67ee9f), from a PC under Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8, BlueZ 5.72 as shipped).
The tests of the report above were run again from Linux. What they add:
  Linux is not affected by bug 1, and bug 2 shows there as from the other hosts. What a Linux host needs in order to pair is on its own side, and goes in the documentation (section 7).
  Three more firmware bugs, numbered 4 to 6 after the three above. All three exist on unmodified master and develop. Each has its fix in commits of its own on the branch, outside the patch of section 6.
  # | Bug | Seen on | Proposed change | 
  4 | A reset while flysight.txt is being written makes the FlySight draw new BLE keys, and the rest of the file is lost | master, develop | state.c, FS_State_Write(): write a second file, then put it in place of the first | 
  5 | A file command that arrives right behind the last acknowledgement of a file read is dropped without an answer | master, develop | crs.c, FS_CRS_State_Read(): stop at the last acknowledgement | 
  6 | A microSD card powered again about 1 ms after losing power leaves the firmware in Error_Handler() | master, develop | resource_manager.c, VCC_DeInit(): keep the supply off for 50 ms | 
Each section below is glossary, problem, proposed fix, tests.
Contents of the Linux part
  7. Linux: bugs 1 and 2 from a Linux PC, and what a Linux host needs to pair
  8. Linux, bug 4: a reset while flysight.txt is being written changes the BLE keys
  9. Linux, bug 5: a command dropped behind the last file acknowledgement
  10. Linux, bug 6: a microSD card powered again too soon locks the FlySight
7.Linux: bugs 1 and 2 from a Linux PC, and what a Linux host needs to pair
Glossary
  BlueZ
  The Bluetooth stack of Linux. An application talks to it over D-Bus.
  Pairing agent
  An object that an application registers with BlueZ (org.bluez.AgentManager1.RegisterAgent), and that BlueZ asks to accept a pairing.
  Library, SkyGames
  "Library" is the native BLE layer of the SkyGames desktop application, driven by a script. "SkyGames" is the application itself.
Problem
Bugs 1 and 2. Linux is not affected by bug 1. The firmware sees the PC connect from its public identity address, with no RPA: the same kind of connection as the Mac's. It is accepted with and without the fix of bug 1, on the four builds of table C and on the instrumented build with the Device Privacy call switched off and on. That is the difference with the Mac: with its default configuration (Privacy off) a Linux host gives the FlySight no identity resolving key when it bonds, and the specification makes a controller ignore the identity address only of a peer that has given one. Bug 2 shows from Linux exactly as from the other hosts.
The first pairing. What stops a Linux host is on its own side. Without a pairing agent registered by the application, BlueZ refuses the pairing, whether it is triggered by reading FT_Packet_In or requested explicitly: the firmware records PAIRING_COMPLETE with status 2 and reason 0x0c, and closes the link at its 30-second timeout. With an agent, the pairing completes and the PC is bonded.
Proposed fix
Nothing to change in the firmware. One line in Docs/ble.md, where pairing is described (commit 85c9a84, Docs: BlueZ needs a pairing agent):
Docs/ble.md
[code]
In the file it is a single line; it is folded here.
Tests
Table C. Linux. The four builds of table B, cable unplugged, from the Linux PC, bonded with the board beforehand. "Library" is the native BLE layer of the SkyGames desktop application driven by a script: it connects, reads FT_Packet_In and sends a ping. "SkyGames" is the application itself; "connects" means it shows the device as connected and has read its configuration file.
  Firmware | Linux library connects, FlySight idle | Linux library connects, FlySight in pairing mode | SkyGames app conn

p='export_conversation.py'; s=open(p).read()
old='''    (re.compile(r"[device id]"), "[device id]"),
]'''
new='''    (re.compile(r"[device id][0-9a-f]*"), "[device id]"),
    # fragments of the identifiers above, as the scans of this very export quote them
    (re.compile(r"[hostname]"), "[hostname]"),
    (re.compile(r"guillaume\\\\?[.-]imbert[@-]c(?![a-z])"), "[user]"),
]'''
if 'fragments of the identifiers' not in s:
    assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new); open(p,'w').write(s)
PY
sed -n 34,39p export_conversation.py | cut -c1-110; T="$HOME/.claude/projects/$(ls $HOME/.claude/projects | grep flysight-2-firmware | head -1)/2eddf3b0-b561-43cc-bb60-c5358363f450.jsonl"; C=$(python3 export_conversation.py "$T" part2_v3.md | sed 's/} [0-9]*$/}/'); echo "$C"; python3 assemble2.py part2_v3.md "$C"; cd ~/dev/Flysight/flysight-2-firmware; L=$(grep -n "^# Second session: Linux" debug_ble/conversation.md | head -1 | cut -d: -f1); python3 - $L <<'PY'
import re, sys, subprocess
L=int(sys.argv[1]); lines=open('debug_ble/conversation.md').read().split('\n')
second='\n'.join(lines[L-1:])
uid=subprocess.run(['id','-u'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.strip()
host=subprocess.run(['hostname'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.strip()
import os
user=os.environ['USER']; dom=user.split('@')[1].split('.')[0]
pats={'uid':uid,'host':host,'host tail':host.split('-')[-1],'login':user,'domain':dom,'device id':'0019003534'+'30'}
for k,v in pats.items(): print('%-10s %d' % (k, len(re.findall(re.escape(v), second, re.I))))
print('key values', len(re.findall(r'BLE_[IE]RK:\s*[0-9a-fA-F]{8}', second)), '| secrets', len(re.findall(r'AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{25}|GOCSPX-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10}|-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE|ya29\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20}', second)))
head=subprocess.run(['git','show','HEAD:debug_ble/conversation.md'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.split('\n')
print('first session untouched:', head[:L-3]==lines[:L-3])
PY
